orgs.n: P2 Masonic lodge secretly enrolled Italy's spy chiefs and MPs
orgs.d: Propaganda Due (P2), a Masonic lodge (a Freemasons' chapter) run by Licio Gelli, secretly enrolled the heads of Italy's intelligence services along with officers, MPs and ministers. On 17 March 1981 police found a list of 962 names at his Villa Wanda in Arezzo, including the heads of all three intelligence services (SISMI, SISDE, CESIS), about 195 military and security officers, 44 members of parliament, three ministers and banker Michele Sindona. Law no. 17 of 25 January 1982 dissolved it; the Anselmi parliamentary commission reported in 1984. In Argentina, junta member Emilio Massera and minister José López Rega were members.
orgs.cite: Italian Parliamentary Commission of Inquiry into the P2 Lodge (Anselmi Commission), 1984; Law 17/1982; Wikipedia 'Propaganda Due'
orgs.reach_src: Countries where P2 had lodges or members, per Wikipedia 'Propaganda Due' (drawing on the Anselmi Commission and later histories).

orgs.n: Freemasons among UK police and judges had to declare membership
orgs.d: The United Grand Lodge of England, the governing body of most English Freemasonry, has members among police officers, judges and magistrates, which led the British government to require them to declare it. In the 1990s Home Secretary Jack Straw required police officers, judges and magistrates who were Freemasons to declare their membership; in 2009 Straw dropped the rule for judges and magistrates, reportedly over fear of losing at the European Court of Human Rights. The Grand Lodge has over 200,000 members in more than 6,800 lodges (local chapters). Its roots go to four London lodges in 1717, and its Grand Master since 1967 is Prince Edward, Duke of Kent.
orgs.cite: UK Home Office disclosure rule (1998) and its withdrawal (2009); Wikipedia 'United Grand Lodge of England'
orgs.reach_src: UGLE says it runs 33 overseas District Grand Lodges, but the source used does not name them; only the home jurisdiction is listed as documented.

orgs.n: Grand Orient de France files decided French army promotions
orgs.d: France's largest Masonic body, the Grand Orient de France, counted many governing politicians among its members and supplied files on army officers that the War Ministry secretly used to decide promotions. In the 1904 Affaire des Fiches ('affair of the index cards') it was revealed that the ministry had used Grand Orient files recording officers' religious and political views to block Catholics from promotion. Under the Third Republic many Radical and later Socialist politicians were members. The Grand Orient was formed in 1773; in 1877 it dropped the requirement to believe in a Supreme Being, and the United Grand Lodge of England has not recognised it since.
orgs.cite: Affaire des Fiches, Chamber of Deputies debate 1904; Wikipedia 'Grand Orient de France'
orgs.reach_src: Lodges outside France named in Wikipedia 'Grand Orient de France'.

orgs.n: Afrikaner Broederbond enrolled every apartheid-era leader
orgs.d: The Afrikaner Broederbond ('Afrikaner Brotherhood'), a secret society of Afrikaner Calvinist men, counted every South African prime minister and state president from 1948 to 1994, the years of National Party and apartheid rule, among its members. It was founded in 1918 as Jong Zuid Afrika and renamed in 1920, when it had 37 members. Ivor Wilkins and Hans Strydom's 1978 book 'The Super-Afrikaners' exposed its membership, listing about 7,500 names; other counts run from 6,800 to 12,000 in about 450 branches. Its last chairman, Tom de Beer (1993–94), went on to chair its successor, the Afrikanerbond.
orgs.cite: Wilkins & Strydom, The Super-Afrikaners (1978); Wikipedia 'Afrikaner Broederbond'

orgs.n: Skull and Bones members reached the US presidency
orgs.d: Skull and Bones, a secret senior society at Yale University, has had members reach the top of the US government. It picks 15 students a year. Members who reached national office include Presidents William Howard Taft, George H. W. Bush and George W. Bush, and Secretary of State John Kerry, who ran against fellow member George W. Bush in 2004. It was founded in December 1832 by William Huntington Russell and Alphonso Taft. It has one chapter and no documented presence abroad.

orgs.n: Bohemian Club gathers presidents and cabinet officers in private
orgs.hq: San Francisco; camp at Bohemian Grove, Sonoma County
orgs.d: The Bohemian Club, a private men's club in San Francisco, brings US presidents, cabinet officers and business leaders together at a closed two-week camp each year at Bohemian Grove in Sonoma County. Members have included several US presidents, usually before election, and many cabinet officers; Richard Nixon was an honorary member. A memo has linked Ronald Reagan's 1983 Social Security cuts to a Bohemian Club meeting in 1981. Journalists founded the club in April 1872, and wealthy and powerful men came to control it.

orgs.n: Ku Klux Klan put members and allies into US public office
orgs.d: The Ku Klux Klan, a white-supremacist secret order, got members and allies into state and federal office during its 1920s revival, when it had an estimated 3–6 million members. In Indiana it backed Edward Jackson's 1924 win for governor; its Grand Dragon (state leader) D. C. Stephenson led it in 22 northern states until his 1925 murder conviction. Hugo Black gave over 100 speeches to Klan meetings during his 1926 Senate race and was appointed to the US Supreme Court in 1937. Violence by the first Klan (1865–1872) led Congress to pass the Enforcement Acts of 1870–71, including the Ku Klux Klan Act.
orgs.reach_src: Wikipedia 'Ku Klux Klan' (Saskatchewan organisers 1926–28 and influence in the provincial Conservative party).

orgs.n: Black Hand officers worked from inside Serbia's army
orgs.d: The Black Hand, a secret society of Serbian army officers, used its members' posts inside the army to overthrow rulers and organise killings abroad. Its leader, Colonel Dragutin Dimitrijević ('Apis'), had led the May 1903 coup in which officers killed King Alexander Obrenović and Queen Draga in Belgrade. The society's constitution was signed on 9 May 1911; members were organised in cells of three to five, with hundreds by 1914. Apis allegedly ordered the 1914 assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo: three young Bosnian Serbs were recruited, trained and smuggled into Bosnia. Whether Apis was involved, and whether the executive committee approved it, is disputed.

orgs.n: Thule Society
orgs.d: The Thule Society was a German nationalist and occultist lodge formed in Munich in 1918, and some of its members later rose to the top of the Nazi state. Historian Nicholas Goodrick-Clarke counts Rudolf Hess and Hans Frank as members, and Alfred Rosenberg, Dietrich Eckart and Gottfried Feder only as guests; he calls longer lists that include Hitler 'spurious'. The society sponsored the German Workers' Party, which became the Nazi Party (NSDAP) by 1920, and it dissolved about 1925. Hess became Deputy Führer in 1933, and Frank became a Reich minister and, from 1939, Governor-General of occupied Poland.
orgs.cite: Goodrick-Clarke, The Occult Roots of Nazism; Wikipedia 'Thule Society'

orgs.n: Opus Dei members served as ministers under Franco
orgs.d: Members of Opus Dei, a Catholic institution, served as government ministers in Spain under the dictator Francisco Franco, including Alberto Ullastres. Historians Paul Preston and Brian Crozier argue they were picked for skill, not membership. Josemaría Escrivá founded Opus Dei in Madrid on 2 October 1928, and its headquarters moved to Rome in 1946. It reported 95,318 members in 2018 (about 85,000 in 2025). Pope Francis's decree Ad charisma tuendum (in force 4 August 2022) moved its oversight to the Vatican's Dicastery for the Clergy and barred its head from becoming a bishop.
orgs.cite: Opus Dei, 'Regional Circumscriptions of Opus Dei'; Ad charisma tuendum (2022); Wikipedia 'Opus Dei'
orgs.reach_src: Opus Dei's own list of countries in its regional circumscriptions (opusdei.org). Hong Kong, Macau, Puerto Rico and Taiwan are also listed there but are not on the canonical country list; 'Congo' on that list is unspecified.

orgs.n: Institute for the Works of Religion (Vatican Bank, IOR)
orgs.d: The Institute for the Works of Religion (IOR), known as the Vatican Bank, is the Holy See's bank, and it was the main shareholder of Italy's Banco Ambrosiano. The IOR was tied to the offshore companies that held the money missing when Ambrosiano collapsed in 1982; Ambrosiano's chairman, Roberto Calvi, belonged to the secret P2 Masonic lodge. In February 1987 Milan magistrates sought the arrest of IOR president Archbishop Paul Marcinkus and two IOR officials, but Italy's top court ruled that the 1929 Lateran Treaty between Italy and the Holy See shielded them. The IOR denied legal liability, acknowledged 'moral involvement' and paid US$224 million to Ambrosiano's creditors in 1984.
orgs.cite: 1984 IOR settlement with Ambrosiano creditors; Vatican tribunal 2021; Wikipedia 'Institute for the Works of Religion'

orgs.n: Communion and Liberation's spokesman governed Lombardy
orgs.d: Communion and Liberation (CL), a Catholic lay movement, had one of its own as governor of Lombardy, Italy's richest region: Roberto Formigoni, who acted as an informal CL political spokesman. In December 2016 a Milan court sentenced Formigoni to six years for bribery and corruption. Fr. Luigi Giussani founded the movement in Milan in 1954; it says it is present in about 90 countries and runs the annual Rimini Meeting, a large political and cultural gathering.
orgs.cite: Milan court verdict on Formigoni, 2016; Wikipedia 'Communion and Liberation'
orgs.reach_src: The source gives '90 countries' with no list; only Italy is documented here.

orgs.n: Unification Church paid South Korean politicians for favours
orgs.d: The Unification Church paid South Korean politicians and the president's wife to win favours for the church, a Seoul court found. On 31 August 2026 it sentenced church leader Han Hak-ja, arrested in September 2025, to two years in prison for giving a high-end necklace and a designer handbag to first lady Kim Keon-hee in July 2022 through an intermediary, and for paying 100 million won to ruling-party lawmaker Kweon Seong-dong in January 2022. She was also convicted of illegal political donations of 144 million won from church funds; both sides are appealing. Sun Myung Moon founded the church in Seoul in 1954; its US arm founded The Washington Times.
orgs.cite: Tokyo District Court dissolution order 25 Mar 2025; Seoul special counsel indictment Oct 2025; Wikipedia 'Unification Church'; Korea Times, 'Unification Church leader sentenced to 2-year prison term in bribery case', 31 Aug 2026; Korea JoongAng Daily on Han's appeal
orgs.reach_src: Countries with named activity in Wikipedia 'Unification Church'; the church says it is in about 100 countries.

orgs.n: Scientology agents planted inside US government agencies
orgs.d: The Church of Scientology placed its own agents in US government agencies to copy files about the church. Under Operation Snow White (1973–77), run by its Guardian's Office (world HQ at Saint Hill Manor, England), agents infiltrated or targeted 136 government agencies, embassies and private bodies in more than 30 countries, including the Internal Revenue Service (the US tax authority) and the Justice Department. After FBI raids on 8 July 1977, eleven senior officials, including Mary Sue Hubbard (five years, $10,000 fine), were convicted in 1979. In Canada the church itself was convicted in 1992 of breach of public trust for infiltrating public offices.
orgs.cite: United States v. Hubbard (D.D.C. 1979); R. v. Church of Scientology of Toronto (1992); Paris criminal court 2009; Wikipedia 'Operation Snow White'
orgs.reach_src: Countries with Scientology organisations, official inquiries or court cases named in Wikipedia 'Scientology' and 'Operation Snow White'.

orgs.n: Gülen followers placed in Turkey's police, courts and army
orgs.d: Followers of the Islamic preacher Fethullah Gülen moved into Turkey's police, prosecution service, courts and army over decades and, Turkish authorities say, used those posts for the movement. A 17 December 2013 corruption probe by police and prosecutors seen as Gülen-aligned forced four ministers to resign. Turkey designated the movement a terrorist group in May 2016 and blamed it for the 15 July 2016 coup attempt; afterwards over 150,000 officials were dismissed and 2,745 judges were purged by the next morning. By 2010 the movement ran over 1,000 schools in more than 100 countries. Gülen, who denied involvement in the coup attempt, died in Pennsylvania in October 2024.
orgs.cite: Turkish National Security Council designation 2016; Statutory decrees 2016; Maarif Foundation statement 2021 (Turkish Minute); Wikipedia 'Gülen movement'
orgs.reach_src: Countries with Gülen-linked schools named in Wikipedia 'Gülen movement'; Maarif takeover counts from Turkish Minute (2021). 'Congo' in the source is unspecified.

orgs.n: Muslim Brotherhood movement put its members in power
orgs.d: The Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist movement founded in Egypt, has put its members into government through its parties and offshoots. Its Freedom and Justice Party won Egypt's presidency in 2012 with Mohamed Morsi, who was overthrown in 2013; Egypt declared the Brotherhood a terrorist group that December, followed by Saudi Arabia and the UAE in March 2014. Sudan's National Islamic Front, a Brotherhood offshoot, took power after the 1989 coup, and Hamas began as an offshoot in 1987. Hassan al-Banna founded the movement in Ismailia in March 1928. Jordan banned it in April 2025, and in January 2026 the US designated three branches as terrorist groups.
orgs.cite: Egyptian cabinet designation Dec 2013; US State/Treasury designations 13 Jan 2026 (Times of Israel); Wikipedia 'Muslim Brotherhood'
orgs.reach_src: National branches and affiliates named in Wikipedia 'Muslim Brotherhood' and the 2026 US designations. Hamas (Palestine) is not on the canonical country list.

orgs.n: Hizb ut-Tahrir members allegedly joined army coup plots
orgs.d: Hizb ut-Tahrir, a pan-Islamist party that aims to restore a caliphate (a single Islamic state under one ruler), has allegedly tried to take power through members involved in military coup plots. It was allegedly behind failed coup attempts in Jordan and Syria in 1968–69 and in Egypt in 1974; a 2004 Nixon Center report cited credible reports of members in coup plots in Jordan, Syria, Egypt, Tunisia and Iraq. Taqi al-Din al-Nabhani founded it in Jerusalem in 1953, and it has spread to more than 50 countries. It is banned in many, including Russia, Pakistan, Germany, Turkey, the UK and Indonesia (status revoked July 2017).
orgs.cite: National bans; Nixon Center report 2004; Wikipedia 'Hizb ut-Tahrir'
orgs.reach_src: Countries where it operates or has been banned (a ban implies presence), per Wikipedia 'Hizb ut-Tahrir'.

orgs.n: Hojjatieh sympathisers held top posts in Iran
orgs.d: The Hojjatieh Society, a Shia religious society, had people with past ties or sympathies in top posts after Iran's 1979 revolution, including Ali Khamenei, Ali Akbar Velayati and Mohammad Ali Rajaei; after 1983 members reportedly worked in the judiciary and security services. The Mashhad cleric Mahmoud Halabi founded it in Tehran in 1953 to oppose the Bahá'í Faith, and it had about 12,000 members by 1977. Khomeini criticised it on 12 July 1983 and Halabi suspended its activities the same day, though it reportedly revived quietly in the 1990s.
orgs.reach_src: Wikipedia 'Hojjatieh' (activity in neighbouring countries by the 1970s, not named).

orgs.n: RSS full-time workers became India's prime ministers
orgs.d: The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), a Hindu nationalist volunteer organisation, has had its own full-time organisers (pracharaks) become prime minister of India: Atal Bihari Vajpayee and Narendra Modi. K. B. Hedgewar founded it in Nagpur on 27 September 1925; its 2019 report counted 84,877 local branches (shakhas). India banned it after Gandhi's assassination in 1948 (lifted July 1949), during the 1975–77 Emergency, and after the 1992 Babri Masjid demolition. Its overseas arm, the Hindu Swayamsevak Sangh, began in Nairobi in 1947 and says it is active in 156 countries.
orgs.cite: Government of India ban orders 1948, 1975, 1992; Wikipedia 'Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh', 'Hindu Swayamsevak Sangh'
orgs.reach_src: RSS in India; Hindu Swayamsevak Sangh branches named in Wikipedia 'Hindu Swayamsevak Sangh' (which claims 156 countries).

orgs.n: Nippon Kaigi members filled 15 of 19 seats in Abe's cabinet
orgs.d: Nippon Kaigi ('Japan Conference'), a nationalist lobby, had 15 of the 19 members of Shinzo Abe's third cabinet among its members after the 2014 reshuffle, and Abe himself was listed as a 'special adviser'. It also runs a league of members of parliament. It was formed on 30 May 1997 by merging two groups, and it claims about 40,000 members in 47 prefectural and about 230 local chapters.

orgs.n: Soka Gakkai's party Komeito sat in Japan's government
orgs.d: Soka Gakkai, a lay Buddhist movement, founded its own party, Komeito, which sat in Japan's government as the Liberal Democratic Party's junior coalition partner from 1999 until the coalition ended in 2025. Daisaku Ikeda, the movement's leader, founded Komeito in 1964. Soka Gakkai was founded on 18 November 1930 by Tsunesaburō Makiguchi and Jōsei Toda. It claims 8.27 million member households in Japan; scholar Levi McLaughlin estimated under 4 million individuals in 2018. A 1995 French parliamentary report listed it among 173 groups it called cults.
orgs.cite: French National Assembly report on cults 1995; Wikipedia 'Soka Gakkai'
orgs.reach_src: Wikipedia 'Soka Gakkai'; Soka Gakkai International claims many more countries, not listed in the source.

orgs.n: Shincheonji Church of Jesus
orgs.d: Shincheonji Church of Jesus is a South Korean religious movement founded by Lee Man-hee in 1984, and investigators found it signed up tens of thousands of its members to the governing People Power Party (PPP). Party members vote in choosing candidates, so mass sign-ups give a group weight inside a party. A joint prosecutor-police team counted at least 56,472 Shincheonji members registered with the PPP between July 2021 and August 2023, including 6,482 in July 2021 alone. Lee was arrested on 24 June 2026 and, with seven other leaders, indicted on 13 July 2026 under the Political Parties Act, which bars forcing anyone to join a party.
orgs.cite: Suwon District Court 2021; Supreme Court of Korea 2022; Wikipedia 'Shincheonji Church of Jesus'
orgs.reach_src: Wikipedia 'Shincheonji Church of Jesus' (the church claims MOUs in 84 countries).

orgs.n: The Fellowship built private ties with lawmakers in the US and Uganda
orgs.d: The Fellowship (also called The Family), a Christian political network, built private ties with lawmakers through prayer groups, the National Prayer Breakfast and a members' house in Washington. It organised the breakfast from 1953, attended by every president since Eisenhower, until it held a separate event in 2023. Its C Street house lodged members of Congress, several tied to 2009 scandals (Sen. John Ensign, Gov. Mark Sanford). Journalist Jeff Sharlet tied Fellowship associates to Uganda's proposed bill making homosexuality punishable by death. Kremlin agent Maria Butina helped arrange Russian attendance at the 2017 breakfast. Abraham Vereide founded it in Seattle in 1935.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'The Fellowship (Christian organization)'; Sharlet, The Family (2008)

orgs.n: El Yunque: alleged secret society inside Mexico's ruling party
orgs.d: El Yunque ('The Anvil') is an alleged secret Catholic far-right society whose members, critics say, held posts in Mexico's National Action Party (PAN) and in President Vicente Fox's cabinet without declaring membership. Journalist Álvaro Delgado first described it in his 2003 book, saying it was founded in Puebla in the early 1950s. Named figures, including Governor Juan Manuel Oliva, denied it. In 2014 a Madrid judge said evidence possibly linked members of the Spanish group HazteOír to El Yunque but could not confirm the organisation exists. Nearly all claims come from critics and ex-members, so its reach is unproven.
orgs.cite: Delgado, El Yunque (2003); Madrid court ruling 2014; Wikipedia 'El Yunque (organization)'

orgs.n: Ordo Iuris Institute for Legal Culture
orgs.d: Ordo Iuris Institute for Legal Culture is a Polish conservative Catholic legal think tank, founded in 2013, that drafts laws and campaigns to change policy, and its co-founder was placed in senior state posts. Aleksander Stępkowski chaired Ordo Iuris's board, then in November 2015 the new Law and Justice government made him deputy foreign minister for legal and treaty affairs; he left in August 2016. In 2016 Ordo Iuris drafted a near-total abortion ban that the Sejm, Poland's lower house, rejected after nationwide protests. Stępkowski was appointed to the Supreme Court in 2019 with no judicial experience and in May 2020 President Andrzej Duda made him its acting First President.

orgs.n: Iglesia ni Cristo
orgs.d: Iglesia ni Cristo (INC) is a Philippine church, founded in 1914, that tells its members to vote as a bloc for candidates it chooses, and it has gained posts and allies inside government in return. After backing Rodrigo Duterte in 2016, its executive minister (head), Eduardo Manalo, was made the president's special envoy for overseas Filipinos in 2018. It helped elect its own member Rodante Marcoleta to the Senate in 2025. When the Ombudsman, who investigates public officers, moved to charge Marcoleta over 75 million pesos in undeclared campaign contributions, the church held a rally of about 12,000 people in Manila on 30 June 2026.
orgs.cite: Philippine Senate resolution 2018; Wikipedia 'Iglesia ni Cristo'
orgs.reach_src: The INC directory (72 states) is cited in Wikipedia but not listed there.

orgs.n: Aum Shinrikyo recruited Japanese soldiers and police officers
orgs.d: Aum Shinrikyo, a Japanese religious group, recruited members from the Japan Self-Defense Forces (Japan's armed forces) and the Tokyo Metropolitan Police. Shoko Asahara founded it in Tokyo in 1987, growing out of a 1984 yoga school. Its sarin nerve-gas attacks killed eight people in Matsumoto in 1994 and 14 on the Tokyo subway in 1995. Asahara and 12 others were executed in July 2018. Russia, Japan, Canada, France and the EU designate it a terrorist group (an official listing that bans support for it); Russia banned it in 2016 and Montenegro expelled 58 linked foreigners that year. It survives as Aleph and Hikari no Wa.
orgs.cite: Tokyo District Court verdicts; Wikipedia 'Aum Shinrikyo'

orgs.n: NATO's secret 'stay-behind' networks inside European states
orgs.hq: NATO Clandestine Planning Committee (SHAPE) and Allied Clandestine Committee; national HQs e.g. Rome
orgs.d: NATO and Western intelligence services set up secret armed 'stay-behind' networks inside European countries after 1945, meant to resist a Soviet invasion, without most parliaments knowing. They were coordinated by NATO's Clandestine Planning Committee (from about 1949–52) and the Allied Clandestine Committee (from 1958), which per the Belgian inquiry covered ten countries. Italian Prime Minister Giulio Andreotti disclosed Italy's network, Gladio, to parliament on 24 October 1990, gave a list of 622 members and said 127 arms caches had been dismantled. The European Parliament on 22 November 1990 called for all such networks to be investigated; Italy, Belgium and Switzerland (P-26) held inquiries.
orgs.cite: Andreotti statement to the Chamber of Deputies 24 Oct 1990; European Parliament resolution 22 Nov 1990; Belgian and Swiss parliamentary reports 1990–91
orgs.reach_src: National stay-behind networks documented in Wikipedia 'Operation Gladio' (Italy Gladio; Denmark Absalon; Greece LOK/Sheepskin; Turkey Counter-Guerrilla; Switzerland P-26; Austria OeWSGV; France Plan Bleu etc.).

orgs.n: Ergenekon (alleged network)
orgs.d: Ergenekon is the name prosecutors gave an alleged secret 'deep state' network in Turkey; the infiltration claim on this map is about who ran the case against it. Turkey's government says followers of the Gülen movement, a religious network led by the preacher Fethullah Gülen, had placed themselves in the police and courts and used those posts to prosecute 275 people from 2008. On 21 April 2016 Turkey's top appeals court overturned the convictions, finding no proof Ergenekon existed and that evidence came from illegal wiretaps and searches; 235 defendants were acquitted at a 2019 retrial. The Gülenist role is the government's claim, not a court finding.
orgs.cite: Istanbul 13th High Criminal Court 2013; Court of Cassation 2016; Wikipedia 'Ergenekon trials'

orgs.n: World Anti-Communist League (now World League for Freedom and Democracy)
orgs.hq: Taipei (HQ); founded as APACL in Jinhae, South Korea
orgs.d: The World Anti-Communist League (WACL), founded in 1954 and called the World League for Freedom and Democracy since 1991, was an international network of governments, parties and armed groups set up to fight communism, and some of its leaders held top state posts. Mario Sandoval Alarcón, a WACL leader and founder of Guatemala's National Liberation Movement, was Guatemala's vice-president from 1974 to 1978. In Argentina, General Carlos Guillermo Suárez Mason chaired the WACL's Latin American chapter while serving as a senior army general and in 1980 became chairman of the Joint Military Chiefs. The League also helped aid Nicaragua's Contra rebels.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'World League for Freedom and Democracy'; 'Iran–Contra affair'; Anderson & Anderson, Inside the League (1986)
orgs.reach_src: Founding states and named national chapters/affiliates (incl. Mexico's Tecos) in Wikipedia 'World League for Freedom and Democracy'. Taiwan (HQ) is not on the canonical country list.

orgs.n: BCCI secretly bought control of a Washington bank
orgs.d: The Bank of Credit and Commerce International (BCCI) secretly controlled First American Bankshares, a Washington bank chaired by former US Defense Secretary Clark Clifford, through nominee owners while hiding its stake from US regulators. BCCI was founded in 1972 by Agha Hasan Abedi, registered in Luxembourg with head offices in Karachi and London, and within a decade had over 400 branches in 78 countries; it handled accounts for Panama's Manuel Noriega. A Luxembourg court ordered it liquidated (closed and its assets sold) on 5 July 1991; losses are estimated at $10–17 billion. Senators John Kerry and Hank Brown reported on it to the Senate Foreign Relations Committee in 1992.
orgs.cite: Kerry–Brown report, 'The BCCI Affair', US Senate 1992; Luxembourg liquidation order 1991
orgs.reach_src: Countries named in Wikipedia 'BCCI' (also Cayman Islands and Hong Kong, not on canonical list). The bank said it operated in 78 countries.

orgs.n: Le Cercle chairs included MPs who did not declare the role
orgs.d: Le Cercle, an invitation-only foreign-policy forum, has been chaired by serving British politicians, including the sitting MPs Rory Stewart and Nadhim Zahawi, who did not declare the role to Parliament. Other chairmen included Brian Crozier, Julian Amery, Jonathan Aitken and Norman Lamont. French prime minister Antoine Pinay and intelligence agent Jean Violet founded it in 1952–53, with Konrad Adenauer and Franz Josef Strauss. Apartheid South Africa sent the only official delegation, and the group backed the Renamo and UNITA rebels. Alan Clark wrote in his diaries that it was CIA-funded.
orgs.reach_src: Founding and 1969 member countries and the South African delegation, per Wikipedia 'Le Cercle'.

orgs.n: Bilderberg dinner promoted the EU Council president's candidacy
orgs.hq: Rotating; first meeting Hotel de Bilderberg, Oosterbeek
orgs.d: The Bilderberg Meetings, a private annual conference of politicians, business leaders and officials, has been used to promote a candidate for a top international post out of public view. In November 2009 a Bilderberg dinner at Val-Duchesse in Brussels promoted Herman Van Rompuy's candidacy for President of the European Council (the post that chairs summits of EU leaders), which he won. The first meeting was held in May 1954 at the Hotel de Bilderberg in Oosterbeek, promoted by Prince Bernhard of the Netherlands. It typically has 120–150 participants; at the 2025 Stockholm meeting, Swedish prime minister Ulf Kristersson attended though not on the published list.
orgs.reach_src: Host countries of documented meetings and nationalities of chairs/attendees named in Wikipedia 'Bilderberg Meeting' and Polskie Radio (2025). The full 23-country 2025 list was not available.

orgs.n: Trilateral Commission members staffed the Carter administration
orgs.d: The Trilateral Commission, a private forum of business and political figures from North America, Western Europe and Japan, supplied much of Jimmy Carter's administration. In 1980 the Christian Science Monitor counted 21 former members in the Carter administration, including Carter himself, Vice-President Walter Mondale, National Security Adviser Zbigniew Brzezinski and Defense Secretary Harold Brown. It was founded in 1973 at David Rockefeller's insistence. Its 2022 European and global membership list covered 38 countries.
orgs.cite: Christian Science Monitor, 17 Apr 1980; Wikipedia 'List of members of the Trilateral Commission'
orgs.reach_src: Member nationalities in Wikipedia 'List of members of the Trilateral Commission' (Aug 2022 list) plus US and Japan from founding regions.

orgs.n: Council on Foreign Relations wrote secret papers for US State Dept
orgs.hq: Harold Pratt House, 58 East 68th Street, New York
orgs.d: The Council on Foreign Relations, a private New York membership body, wrote confidential policy papers for the US State Department during the Second World War and has supplied many of the officials who run US foreign policy. Its War and Peace Studies group, funded by the Rockefeller Foundation, wrote 682 confidential memoranda for the State Department. About 40% of top foreign-policy officials under Eisenhower were members, as were Secretaries of State John Foster Dulles and Cyrus Vance. Incorporated on 29 July 1921, it has published the journal Foreign Affairs since 1922 and had 5,397 members in 2025, open only to US citizens and some permanent residents.
orgs.reach_src: Offices in New York and Washington only.

orgs.n: WEF Young Global Leaders alumni went on to lead governments
orgs.d: The World Economic Forum, a Swiss foundation best known for its annual meeting in Davos, runs a Young Global Leaders programme whose alumni include many later heads of government. The programme, begun in 1992, has inducted about 1,400 people; alumni who later led governments include Justin Trudeau, Emmanuel Macron, Jacinda Ardern, Sanna Marin, Mark Rutte, Alexander De Croo, Sebastian Kurz and Enrique Peña Nieto. Klaus Schwab founded the Forum in 1971 and stepped down as chair on 21 April 2025; an external investigation found no 'material wrongdoing'.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'World Economic Forum', 'Forum of Young Global Leaders'
orgs.reach_src: Headquarters and offices named in Wikipedia 'World Economic Forum' (New York, Beijing, Tokyo, Seoul; C4IR in San Francisco). It also runs 19 Centres for the Fourth Industrial Revolution, not listed in the source.

orgs.n: Mont Pelerin Society members took top economic posts
orgs.hq: Mont Pèlerin, Switzerland (founded); secretariat Lubbock, Texas
orgs.d: The Mont Pelerin Society, a free-market society of economists and thinkers, has had members in top government and central-bank posts. They include President Luigi Einaudi (Italy), Chancellor Ludwig Erhard (West Germany), President Václav Klaus (Czech Republic), Prime Minister Ranil Wickremesinghe (Sri Lanka), Chancellor of the Exchequer Geoffrey Howe (UK), finance ministers Carlos Cáceres (Chile) and Ruth Richardson (New Zealand), Secretary of State George Shultz and Federal Reserve chairman Arthur Burns. Friedrich Hayek founded it on 10 April 1947 at a meeting at Mont Pèlerin, Switzerland, with about 39 invited scholars.
orgs.reach_src: Member countries named in Wikipedia 'Mont Pelerin Society'.

orgs.n: Atlas Network partners write laws and lobby officials abroad
orgs.d: The Atlas Network, a US foundation that sets up and supports free-market think tanks around the world, works through those partners to write legislation and meet policymakers in their countries. Founded in 1981 by Antony Fisher, it calls itself 'a think tank that creates think tanks'. It grew from 15 think tanks in nine countries in the mid-1980s to 581 members in more than 100 countries in 2024. WNYC reported that partners write legislation and meet policymakers; a 2018 academic article said World Bank Doing Business work 'follows exactly Atlas' policy recommendations'. ALEC, which drafts model US state laws, is a member.
orgs.reach_src: Countries of partner organisations named in Wikipedia 'Atlas Network' (the full directory covers 100+ countries).

orgs.n: ALEC: companies and legislators draft 'model bills' for US states
orgs.d: The American Legislative Exchange Council (ALEC) brings corporate members and state legislators together to draft 'model bills', which the legislators then introduce in their own states. By 2011 it had about 2,000 legislator members, over a quarter of US state legislators; about 1,000 bills based on its model language were introduced each year and roughly 20% enacted. After Florida's 2005 'Stand Your Ground' law (allowing deadly force in self-defence without first retreating), ALEC adopted it as a model bill and similar laws spread to about 30 states. Coca-Cola and Microsoft left after the 2012 killing of Trayvon Martin. Paul Weyrich co-founded it in 1973.

orgs.n: China's United Front reached UK MPs through a London solicitor
orgs.d: The United Front Work Department, a department of the Chinese Communist Party, works through overseas Chinese groups and individuals to build influence over foreign politicians. In January 2022 MI5, Britain's security service, warned MPs that London solicitor Christine Lee was suspected of political interference on its behalf; she had given more than £420,000 over five years to Labour MP Barry Gardiner. Neither was accused of a crime, and China denied it. A February 2022 Canadian court ruling found the party's Overseas Chinese Affairs Office engaged in covert intelligence gathering. In 2024 reporters identified 233 people across Europe linked to the united front system.
orgs.cite: MI5 interference alert Jan 2022; Federal Court of Canada 2022; US sanctions Jan 2021; Wikipedia 'United Front Work Department'; The Week, 'Christine Lee: the Chinese spy with links to a Labour MP', Jan 2022
orgs.reach_src: Countries with documented cases in Wikipedia 'United Front Work Department'.

orgs.n: Grey Wolves militia tied to Turkey's secret state forces
orgs.d: The Grey Wolves (Ülkü Ocakları), the youth and paramilitary wing of Turkey's Nationalist Movement Party (MHP), worked with parts of the Turkish state's security apparatus. Former prosecutor Emin Değer documented ties to the Counter-Guerrilla, Turkey's branch of NATO's secret stay-behind network. Its second-in-command Abdullah Çatlı died in the 1996 Susurluk car crash alongside a police chief and an MP, which led to a parliamentary inquiry in 1997. The group was linked to the 1976–80 street violence, including the 1978 Maraş massacre of over 100 Alevis. Since 2018 the MHP has been allied with Erdoğan's AKP; France banned the Grey Wolves in 2020.
orgs.cite: Emin Değer; Susurluk parliamentary inquiry 1997; French decree of dissolution Nov 2020
orgs.reach_src: Wikipedia 'Grey Wolves (organization)' (presence and bans). Northern Cyprus is not on the canonical list.

orgs.n: Uniter network drew in German special-forces soldiers and police
orgs.d: Uniter e.V., an association set up by André Schmitt ('Hannibal'), a soldier from the German army's Special Forces Command (KSK), brought current and former soldiers and police into chat groups preparing for a 'Day X' collapse of public order. Investigators found the chat groups in 2017 while looking into soldiers preparing for Day X. Germany's domestic intelligence agency, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution, classed Uniter internally as a review case by February 2020 and placed it under surveillance in early July 2020. Schmitt was fined under the explosives law after training grenades, smoke cartridges and fuses were found on him.
orgs.reach_src: German authorities' classification and AP reporting.

orgs.n: Congress for Cultural Freedom
orgs.d: The Congress for Cultural Freedom was an anti-communist organisation of writers and intellectuals, founded in West Berlin in 1950, that the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) secretly paid for and ran. It was run from Paris by Michael Josselson, a CIA officer, had offices in 35 countries and published more than 20 magazines, including Encounter and Preuves. The New York Times reported the CIA funding in April 1966, and in 1967 former CIA official Thomas Braden admitted the agency had funded it for more than ten years. It was then renamed the International Association for Cultural Freedom, funded by the Ford Foundation, and dissolved in 1979.
orgs.cite: CIA Center for the Study of Intelligence; Saturday Evening Post (Braden), May 1967
orgs.reach_src: Offices, magazines and conferences listed in CCF/IACF publication lists (Bombay 1951, Rangoon, Mexico City, Tokyo, Ibadan, Copenhagen office 1960, Quadrant in Australia, Transition in Uganda)

orgs.n: Asia Foundation (formerly Committee for a Free Asia)
orgs.d: The Asia Foundation is a US body running education and governance programmes in Asia that the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) created and ran as a 'proprietary', an organisation the CIA secretly owned while it appeared independent. A CIA memorandum of 22 June 1966 describes it as set up in 1954 to do cultural and educational work for the US government 'in ways not open to official U.S. agencies', under the code name DTPILLAR. It grew out of the Committee for a Free Asia (1951). After press disclosures of CIA funding of private groups in 1966–67, the US government decided to keep the foundation and fund it openly.
orgs.reach_src: CIA memorandum (programme countries not listed in the memo)

orgs.n: CIA secretly funded the US National Student Association
orgs.d: The CIA secretly paid for the international programme of the United States National Student Association, a confederation of US college student governments, from the early 1950s to 1967, and used it to help build anti-communist international student bodies. The association was founded at the University of Wisconsin in 1947. Ramparts magazine exposed the funding in February 1967, and the Church Committee (the US Senate inquiry into intelligence abuses) later documented it in 1976. The association cut its CIA ties in August 1967 and merged into the United States Student Association in 1978.
orgs.cite: Ramparts, Feb 1967; Church Committee Book I (1976)

orgs.n: US union committee channelled CIA money into European unions
orgs.d: The American Federation of Labor's Free Trade Union Committee passed money, including CIA funds, to anti-communist trade unions in Western Europe. Created at the AFL's 1944 convention with $1 million and run by Jay Lovestone, with Irving Brown as its man in Paris, it funded France's Force Ouvrière from 1948, Italy's CISL union federation, and anti-communist dockworker groups in French, Italian and Greek ports. Historian Anthony Carew found it carried CIA money for about 20 years, starting with the 1948 Italian election.
orgs.cite: Anthony Carew, Labor History (1998); Ted Morgan, A Covert Life (1999)

orgs.n: US-funded labour institute trained unionists who joined Brazil's coup
orgs.d: The American Institute for Free Labor Development, set up by the US union federation AFL-CIO with business and government partners, trained Latin American union leaders, and its director said Brazilian trainees took part in the 1964 coup that overthrew Brazil's government. It was chartered in August 1962 under the Alliance for Progress (a US aid programme for Latin America) and funded by contracts with USAID, the US aid agency. It trained leaders in their own countries and in the United States. Director William Doherty Jr. said its Brazilian trainees were 'intimately involved' in the coup. In the mid-1990s it was merged into the American Center for International Labor Solidarity.
orgs.cite: Cliff Welch, Latin American Research Review

orgs.n: CIA-linked IBAD paid Brazilian opposition candidates in 1962
orgs.d: The Brazilian Institute of Democratic Action (IBAD), an anti-communist body linked to the CIA and financed by multinational companies, paid for the campaigns of many opposition candidates in Brazil's October 1962 elections, so that politicians it funded would sit in office. A parliamentary inquiry commission investigated it, and President João Goulart closed it in 1963. In 1977 former US ambassador Lincoln Gordon admitted that the US had funded the opposition in that election.
orgs.cite: Brazilian CPI on IBAD (1963); Lincoln Gordon (1977)

orgs.n: Radio Free Europe / Radio Liberty
orgs.d: Radio Free Europe and Radio Liberty were US-run stations broadcasting from Munich into the Soviet bloc that presented themselves as private but were secretly created and funded by the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA). Radio Free Europe was launched in 1949 by the National Committee for a Free Europe, a CIA front organised by Allen Dulles, and Radio Liberty followed in 1951. The CIA and State Department set broad policy for both. After Senator Clifford Case moved in 1971 to take their funding out of the CIA budget, CIA money ended in 1971–72; from 1974 Congress funded them openly. They merged in 1976 and moved to Prague in 1995.
orgs.cite: US Congress (Case bill, 1971); Board for International Broadcasting Act 1973

orgs.n: CIA routed secret money through US private foundations
orgs.d: The CIA's International Organizations Division secretly passed money through US private foundations to labour, youth, student and cultural groups, so that the funds looked like ordinary charitable grants. Thomas Braden headed the division from 1950. The Church Committee (the US Senate inquiry into intelligence abuses, reporting in 1976) found CIA money in at least 108 of 700 large grants made by 164 US foundations in 1963–66, and in nearly half of their international grants. The Katzenbach Committee ended covert funding of US educational and private voluntary groups in 1967.
orgs.cite: Church Committee Final Report, Book I (1976), pp. 182-192

orgs.n: Ford Foundation trained the economists who ran Suharto's economy
orgs.d: The Ford Foundation, a large US private foundation, paid for University of Indonesia economists to train at the University of California, Berkeley from the late 1950s; they then became Suharto's economic ministers. It also funded the second phase (1965–73) of the University of Chicago–Catholic University of Chile programme, whose graduates ran Chile's economy under Pinochet, and took over funding of the Congress for Cultural Freedom's successor after the CIA's role was exposed in 1967.

orgs.n: US-funded 'Chicago Boys' took over Pinochet's economic posts
orgs.d: A US-funded programme linking the University of Chicago's economics department to Santiago's Catholic University trained the Chilean economists, known as the 'Chicago Boys', who held Pinochet's finance, economy and central bank posts from 1975. The US government's Point Four aid scheme set it up in the mid-1950s; between 1955 and 1973, 126 Chilean students trained under it, paid by US aid until 1964 and then the Ford Foundation. Its graduates wrote 'El ladrillo' ('The Brick'), the economic plan the military government adopted.
orgs.cite: Milton and Rose Friedman, Two Lucky People (1998)

orgs.n: International Criminal Police Organization (Interpol)
orgs.d: Interpol is a body of 196 member countries through which police forces ask each other to find and arrest suspects; member governments have placed their own officials at its head. China's Vice-Minister of Public Security, Meng Hongwei, was elected Interpol president in 2016 while still holding that post; he vanished in China in 2018 and was jailed for bribery. The United Arab Emirates (UAE) gave about $54 million through the Interpol Foundation, estimated to equal the yearly dues of all other members combined, and in 2021 its interior ministry official Ahmed Naser Al-Raisi was elected president. A report by former UK prosecutions chief David Calvert-Smith questioned the donations.

orgs.n: Tobacco firms placed consultants inside the WHO
orgs.d: Tobacco companies placed their own consultants in posts at the World Health Organization (the UN health agency) and secretly paid 'independent' experts to undermine its tobacco-control work, an expert committee chaired by Swiss scientist Thomas Zeltner found in 2000. The committee said the placements raised 'serious questions about whether the integrity of WHO decision-making has been compromised'. It found the companies also used academic-style groups whose industry funding was hidden, and lobbied delegates from developing countries to resist anti-tobacco resolutions. In 2010 the Council of Europe's Parliamentary Assembly criticised WHO's H1N1 flu decisions for lack of transparency about industry ties.
orgs.cite: Zeltner Committee report (2000); PACE Res. 1749 (2010); CBS News, 'WHO slams Big Tobacco's global tactics', Aug 2000

orgs.n: FIFA officials took bribes for marketing rights and World Cup votes
orgs.d: Sports-marketing companies paid bribes to officials of FIFA, the world football federation, and its regional bodies to win marketing rights, and officials took bribes over World Cup votes, the US Justice Department charged in 2015. In May 2015 it indicted 14 people, and later dozens more; seven FIFA officials were arrested at Zurich's Baur au Lac hotel on 27 May 2015. Several defendants had held public office: a former President of Honduras, a former governor of São Paulo, a Trinidad cabinet minister and a Guatemalan judge.
orgs.cite: US DOJ press releases, 27 May and 3 Dec 2015
orgs.reach_src: FIFA case defendants who held public office

orgs.n: Olympic bid teams paid IOC members for host-city votes
orgs.d: Cities bidding to host the Olympic Games gave gifts and money to members of the International Olympic Committee, whose votes choose the host. In 1999 the IOC expelled ten members and sanctioned ten others over gifts from the Salt Lake City bid. In 2021 a Brazilian federal court in Rio convicted Carlos Nuzman, head of the Rio 2016 bid, of buying IOC votes, after Rio governor Sérgio Cabral admitted paying $2 million to IOC member Lamine Diack.
orgs.cite: IOC ad hoc commission (1999); 7th Federal Criminal Court, Rio (2021)

orgs.n: Rhodes's secret society and the Milner Group (per Carroll Quigley)
orgs.d: Historian Carroll Quigley wrote that Cecil Rhodes founded a secret society in London in 1891 to extend British rule, and that its circle, later called the Milner Group, placed its members in government. Quigley names Alfred Milner, Reginald Brett (Lord Esher) and W. T. Stead as its 'Junta of Three'. Milner ran British South Africa from 1897 to 1905; Esher's 1904 committee reorganised the War Office; Earl Grey, a Rhodes company director, was Governor General of Canada from 1904 to 1911. The society's existence and membership rest on Quigley.
orgs.cite: Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment (written c. 1949, published 1981), ch. 1 and 3; Tragedy and Hope (1966), pp. 950–952
orgs.reach_src: Countries where Quigley places its members in office; membership itself rests on Quigley

orgs.n: Rhodes Scholarships: a network whose alumni led governments
orgs.d: The Rhodes Trust, set up under the will of the British colonialist Cecil Rhodes to promote unity among English-speaking nations, funds scholarships at Oxford whose alumni include eight later heads of state or government, among them Bill Clinton, John Turner, Bob Hawke, Tony Abbott and Malcolm Turnbull. It was created on Rhodes's death in March 1902, originally for men from the Commonwealth, Germany and the United States; women were admitted from 1977. The first trustees included Alfred Milner, Lord Rosebery, Earl Grey and Alfred Beit; Philip Kerr of Milner's circle was General Secretary 1925–39.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Rhodes Scholarship'; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, ch. 3
orgs.reach_src: Original eligibility and scholar heads of government (Wikipedia); trust founded from Rhodes's South African fortune

orgs.n: Milner's young recruits ran the post-war Transvaal government
orgs.d: Alfred Milner, Britain's High Commissioner in South Africa, recruited young Oxford graduates from 1901 to staff the colonial government of the Transvaal and Orange River Colony after the Boer War; the group, known as Milner's Kindergarten, then used those posts to push for union of the four colonies, achieved in 1910. Members included Lionel Curtis, Philip Kerr, Robert Brand, Geoffrey Dawson and Patrick Duncan. On returning to England in 1909 the group renamed itself the Round Table and continued as a policy network.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Milner's Kindergarten'; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, ch. 4

orgs.n: Round Table movement
orgs.d: The Round Table was a network of British imperialists formed in 1909 by Alfred Milner's former staff to promote imperial unity, and historian Carroll Quigley argues its members were placed in government and the press. Milner sat in Lloyd George's War Cabinet from 1916 to 1918; Philip Kerr, founding editor of the network's journal, joined the Prime Minister's staff in 1916. Lionel Curtis's study group with India Office officials worked out 'dyarchy', the shared rule written into the Government of India Act 1919. Geoffrey Dawson edited The Times during the appeasement of Hitler, and Quigley places Foreign Secretary Lord Halifax in its inner core. The membership claims are Quigley's.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Round Table movement'; Quigley, Tragedy and Hope, pp. 950–951

orgs.n: Royal Institute of International Affairs (Chatham House)
orgs.d: Chatham House, formally the Royal Institute of International Affairs, is a private London foreign-policy institute whose wartime research unit was taken into the Foreign Office. During the Second World War it ran a Foreign Research and Press Service under the historian Arnold Toynbee, and from 1943 to 1946 that service was moved into the Foreign Office, so the institute's staff worked inside the ministry. Chatham House grew from a meeting that Lionel Curtis, a member of Lord Milner's network of imperialists, called in Paris on 30 May 1919; it opened in 1920 and received a royal charter in 1926.
orgs.cite: Chatham House, 'The Hotel Majestic and the Origins of Chatham House' (2019); Wikipedia 'Chatham House'; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, ch. 10

orgs.n: Institute of Pacific Relations
orgs.d: The Institute of Pacific Relations (IPR) was a private research body on Asia, founded in 1925 and funded mainly by the Rockefeller and Carnegie foundations, that others were accused of using to steer US policy. In 1952 the Senate Internal Security Subcommittee under Pat McCarran, after reviewing about 20,000 IPR documents, reported that it 'was a vehicle used by the Communists' to shape US Far East policy; Owen Lattimore, editor of the IPR journal, was a central target. The IRS revoked its tax exemption in 1955, but courts rejected all the IRS allegations in 1959. Historian Carroll Quigley argued that Wall Street money and the Milner Group mattered more.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Institute of Pacific Relations'; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, ch. 10
orgs.reach_src: Senate Internal Security Subcommittee 1952 (State Department policy)

orgs.n: Wagner placed fighters and advisers beside African leaders
orgs.d: The Wagner Group, a Russian mercenary company financed by Yevgeny Prigozhin and used by the Russian state, placed fighters, bodyguards and advisers inside governments in Syria and Africa, paid partly in mining and timber concessions. In the Central African Republic a Russian, Valery Zakharov, served as security adviser to President Faustin-Archange Touadéra; Ukraine's SBU said he was himself a Wagner member, and a November 2021 EU report found most deployed Central African army units operated under Wagner command or supervision. Wagner's African firms included Meroe Gold (Sudan) and Lobaye Invest (CAR). After Prigozhin's death in 2023 most operations moved to Russia's defence ministry.
orgs.cite: US Treasury designations 2020–2023; UN Panel of Experts on Libya (2020); Wikipedia; Wikipedia 'Wagner Group activities in the Central African Republic' (Zakharov; EEAS report Nov 2021)
orgs.reach_src: UN Panel on Libya; US Treasury; Wikipedia country articles

orgs.n: Prigozhin political-technologist and disinformation network (incl. AFRIC)
orgs.d: This was a network of Russian political strategists, social-media operators and front groups paid through companies of Yevgeny Prigozhin, the businessman behind the Wagner Group, that worked to shape who held office in African states from 2018. In Madagascar's 2018 presidential race, Proekt and the BBC reported, 15–20 of these strategists dealt with as many as eight candidates; candidate André Mailhol said he was given €5,000 in cash and ex-prime minister Omer Beriziky said he was promised $2 million. The winner, Andry Rajoelina, denied being Russia's candidate. Facebook removed three of the network's operations targeting eight African states in October 2019.
orgs.cite: Facebook takedown 30 Oct 2019; Stanford Internet Observatory; Proekt/BBC (2019); EPDE (2020)
orgs.reach_src: Facebook Oct 2019 announcement; EPDE AFRIC report

orgs.n: Hezbollah's armed movement sits inside Lebanon's parliament and cabinet
orgs.d: Hezbollah, a Shia Islamist armed movement aligned with Iran's Revolutionary Guards, holds seats in Lebanon's parliament (about 14 of 128) and posts in its cabinet while keeping its own armed wing outside state control. At least 28 countries list that armed wing as terrorist. It is part of Iran's 'Axis of Resistance', a network of allied groups across the Middle East. Since August 2025 the Lebanese cabinet has backed an army plan to disarm it.

orgs.n: Iran's Quds Force placed allied militias inside Iraq's security forces
orgs.d: Iran's Quds Force, the foreign-operations branch of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), arms, trains and directs allied militias, several of which sit inside other countries' official security forces, notably Iraq's Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), a state-paid umbrella of mostly Shia militias. The PMF's deputy head, Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis, also led the Iran-backed militia Kataib Hezbollah and was killed alongside Quds Force commander Qassem Soleimani in a US strike in Baghdad in January 2020. The US listed the IRGC, including the Quds Force, as a Foreign Terrorist Organization in April 2019, and courts in several countries have convicted people described as its operatives.
orgs.cite: US State Department FTO listing (2019); Wikipedia; AP/PBS NewsHour, 'Iraqi militant killed in U.S. strike worked with Iran for decades', 3 Jan 2020; Al Jazeera, 7 Jan 2020

orgs.n: Gupta brothers got South African ministers to act for their firms
orgs.d: The Gupta brothers, Ajay, Atul and Rajesh, and their associate Salim Essa used their closeness to President Jacob Zuma to get ministers and heads of state-owned companies to act for their businesses, a practice South Africans call 'state capture'. Their network was built around Sahara Computers and Oakbay Investments. The Zondo Commission, a judicial inquiry that reported in 2022, found ministers and state-company heads acted corruptly on the network's behalf. The US sanctioned the brothers in 2019 and the UK in 2021. They have lived in Dubai since 2016.

orgs.n: McKinsey bribed South African state-company officials
orgs.d: McKinsey & Company, a US management consultancy, bribed officials at Eskom, South Africa's state power company, and Transnet, its state freight company, in 2012–2016 to win contracts, according to a 2024 US Justice Department settlement. It worked on those contracts alongside Trillian, a firm linked to the Gupta family's state-capture network. McKinsey repaid about R1 billion to Eskom and R870 million to Transnet, and in 2024 paid a $122 million US penalty under a deferred prosecution agreement (a deal in which charges are dropped if the company meets set conditions).
orgs.cite: US Department of Justice (2024); Zondo Commission

orgs.n: Huawei Technologies
orgs.d: Huawei is China's largest telecoms-equipment maker, and prosecutors in Belgium and Poland say people working for it reached inside public bodies. Belgian prosecutors allege that associates of a former Huawei lobbyist gave gifts and payments to members of the European Parliament (MEPs), including up to €15,000 for writing and €1,500 for co-signing a 2021 letter against limits on foreign 5G equipment; eight people have been charged, and in June 2026 Parliament lifted the immunity of MEP Fulvio Martusciello, who denies wrongdoing. In Poland a senior Huawei employee and a former counter-intelligence official were charged in 2019 with spying for China; both pleaded not guilty.

orgs.n: Heritage Foundation's Project 2025 authors took Trump posts
orgs.d: The Heritage Foundation, a conservative think tank in Washington, organised Project 2025, a 900-plus-page plan for a conservative administration written with dozens of partner groups, and several of its authors then took the posts that carry it out. They include Russ Vought, who became director of the Office of Management and Budget (the White House budget office), and Brendan Carr, who became chairman of the Federal Communications Commission (the broadcast and telecoms regulator), in the second Trump administration in 2025.

orgs.n: Center for American Progress staff moved into Biden posts
orgs.d: The Center for American Progress (CAP), a Democratic-leaning Washington think tank, has supplied many officials to Democratic administrations: Business Insider counted nearly 70 former CAP employees in Biden-administration posts by mid-2021, after its staff also moved into the Obama administration. John Podesta founded it on 24 October 2003 as a counterpart to the Heritage Foundation and the American Enterprise Institute. Neera Tanden leads it.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Center for American Progress'; Fox News, 15 September 2022

orgs.n: Federalist Society members filled Trump's appeals-court seats
orgs.d: The Federalist Society, a network of about 70,000 conservative and libertarian lawyers, helped draw up Donald Trump's 2016 Supreme Court shortlist, and 43 of his first 51 appeals-court nominees were members. Appeals courts are the federal courts just below the Supreme Court, and their judges serve for life. The society formed in April 1982 at Yale, Harvard and Chicago law schools. The liberal American Constitution Society was founded in 2001 as its counterpart.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Federalist Society'; New York Times, 16 March 2020

orgs.n: Evangelical churches' voting bloc in Brazil's Congress
orgs.d: The Frente Parlamentar Evangélica is a registered cross-party caucus (a voting bloc of legislators from different parties) inside Brazil's National Congress, through which evangelical churches organise their members in office to push church causes in law. Its vice-president said in February 2023 that 132 deputies and 14 senators had signed on. Agência Pública counted 93 deputies tied to evangelical churches, led by the Assemblies of God, the Baptists and the Universal Church, which shows which churches supply most of the bloc's members.

orgs.n: Colombian church's MIRA party holds seats in Congress
orgs.d: The Church of God Ministry of Jesus Christ International, a Pentecostal church founded in Colombia, has its own political party, MIRA, which puts church members into Colombia's Senate, House of Representatives and local councils. MIRA (Independent Movement of Absolute Renovation) was founded in 2000 and lists the church as its religion. The church therefore reaches lawmaking bodies directly through elected members who answer to the same religious movement, rather than by lobbying from outside.

orgs.n: Confucius Institutes
orgs.d: China's government placed Confucius Institutes, Chinese-language and culture centres, inside foreign universities and schools, funded through its education ministry (formerly via the agency Hanban). A US Senate subcommittee reported in February 2019 that Hanban chose the teachers, who signed contracts promising not to harm China's national interests, and that China had given US universities over $158 million since 2006. The National Association of Scholars counted about 550 institutes worldwide in 2020. The US State Department designated their US centre a foreign mission of China on 13 August 2020, and 104 of 118 US institutes had closed by June 2022.
orgs.cite: RFA, 13 August 2020; The Diplomat, November 2023; US Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, 'China's Impact on the US Education System', February 2019, via RFA, 1 March 2019

orgs.n: Gambling hubs got a mayor with a fake identity into office
orgs.d: Philippine offshore gaming operators (POGOs), online gambling firms mostly owned by Chinese nationals, got their people into Philippine local government: 2024 Senate hearings linked hubs to fake Filipino identities, including that of Bamban mayor Alice Guo, and in August 2024 the Ombudsman (who disciplines officials) dismissed her, ruling she had planned her town's illegal gambling hub and run for mayor to protect it. POGOs were licensed by the regulator PAGCOR to serve players in China, where gambling is illegal; they grew from 2016 under President Duterte to 48,883 workers by 2024. President Marcos ordered all POGOs closed by 31 December 2024 and Congress banned them by law in October 2025.
orgs.cite: Philippine Senate hearings 2024; Executive Order 74 (2024); Anti-POGO Act (2025); Office of the Ombudsman ruling on Alice Guo, via BenarNews, 14 August 2024

orgs.n: Scam-compound tycoon Chen Zhi became adviser to Hun Sen
orgs.d: Chen Zhi, a Fujian-born businessman who became a Cambodian citizen, got inside Cambodia's government as an adviser to Prime Minister Hun Sen while running Prince Holding Group, a property, banking and tourism conglomerate he founded in 2015 in Phnom Penh. On 14 October 2025 the US indicted Chen for running forced-labour scam compounds; prosecutors said he and Prince executives used political influence in several countries and paid bribes to public officials to avoid police action. The US seized about 127,271 bitcoin, the US and UK sanctioned 146 linked people and firms, and Singapore, Taiwan and Hong Kong seized assets. Cambodia sent Chen to China in January 2026.
orgs.cite: US DOJ indictment and OFAC/UK sanctions, 14 October 2025; US Attorney's Office E.D.N.Y. press release on Chen Zhi indictment, 14 October 2025
orgs.reach_src: US/UK sanctions and asset seizures as summarised on Wikipedia

orgs.n: Ma Ba Tha monks drafted Myanmar's race and religion laws
orgs.d: Ma Ba Tha, a Buddhist nationalist monks' organisation formed in Myanmar in January 2014, wrote laws from outside Parliament: its members proposed the texts of four Race and Religion Protection Laws, which restrict interfaith marriage and religious conversion, and Parliament passed them in 2015. The group is linked to the 969 movement and the monk Wirathu. The state clergy council, the government-backed body that oversees Buddhist monks, ordered it disbanded in May 2017, but it continued under new names, and its leading figures have received donations and honours from military leaders.
orgs.cite: Human Rights Watch 2014; State Sangha Maha Nayaka Committee order, May 2017

orgs.n: Bodu Bala Sena leader put in charge of state legal task force
orgs.d: Bodu Bala Sena, a Sinhala Buddhist nationalist organisation of monks founded in Sri Lanka in 2012, got its leader into a state post: in 2021 President Gotabaya Rajapaksa appointed its general secretary, Galagoda Aththe Gnanasara, to chair a government task force on a 'One Country, One Law' legal policy. The tie went back to 2013, when Rajapaksa, then Defence Secretary, opened the group's training centre. Gnanasara has been jailed several times; in 2026 the Supreme Court voided the presidential pardon he received in 2019 and he was returned to prison.
orgs.cite: Daily FT, 27 October 2021; Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, 10 September 2026

orgs.n: Fight Impunity: cash channel to buy influence in EU Parliament
orgs.d: Fight Impunity, a Brussels non-profit set up by former Italian Member of the European Parliament (MEP) Pier Antonio Panzeri, served, according to Belgian investigators, as the channel through which Qatar, Morocco and Mauritania paid cash to influence decisions inside the European Parliament. The case, known as 'Qatargate', came to light when police raided its office on 9 December 2022 and found about €600,000 in cash at Panzeri's home. Panzeri agreed a plea deal in January 2023, admitting his role in exchange for cooperation. The non-profit's largest declared donor was a foundation of South African businessman Iqbal Survé.
orgs.cite: Belgian Federal Prosecutor's Office; Qatargate case file reported by Der Spiegel and Financial Times
orgs.reach_src: Belgian investigation as reported (suspects' nationalities and paying states)

orgs.n: Azerbaijan paid European politicians ('caviar diplomacy')
orgs.d: Azerbaijan's government used gifts, paid trips and cash to buy the votes of European politicians, especially members of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE), a human-rights body that monitors elections and political prisoners; the European Stability Initiative named this 'caviar diplomacy' in 2012. A PACE investigation body reported in April 2018 on breaches by members from several countries. An Italian court jailed former PACE group leader Luca Volontè in 2021, and the Bundestag lifted two members' immunity from prosecution in 2021. The 2017 Azerbaijani Laundromat leak showed $2.9 billion moved through Danske Bank Estonia in 2012–2014, part of it to politicians.
orgs.cite: European Stability Initiative reports 2012 and 2016; PACE Independent Investigation Body report, 2018; OCCRP 2017
orgs.reach_src: PACE investigation body report 2018 and OCCRP laundromat recipients

orgs.n: Salvini aide negotiated secret Russian oil money for the Lega
orgs.d: Gianluca Savoini, president of the Associazione Culturale Lombardia Russia and a long-time aide of Lega leader Matteo Salvini, was recorded at Moscow's Metropol hotel in October 2018 negotiating an oil deal meant to channel Russian money secretly to the Lega, then part of Italy's governing coalition. The association is a Milan cultural group that promotes ties with Russia. Milan prosecutors investigated, and in April 2023 a judge closed the case, finding that the aim was illicit party financing but that the deal never got far enough to count as a crime.
orgs.cite: Milan preliminary-investigations judge, dismissal order of April 2023

orgs.n: Medvedchuk network paid European politicians
orgs.d: Viktor Medvedchuk, a pro-Kremlin Ukrainian politician exchanged to Russia in 2022, paid European politicians to carry Russian positions inside their parliaments. Czech intelligence exposed the Prague-based site Voice of Europe in March 2024 as run for him by Artem Marchevskyi and used to pay European politicians; the EU sanctioned it in May 2024. In the UK, former Member of the European Parliament Nathan Gill was jailed in 2025 for taking bribes in 2018–2019 from Ukrainian MP Oleg Voloshyn, who passed on Medvedchuk's requests for speeches and statements.
orgs.cite: Czech Security Information Service 2024; EU Council sanctions May 2024; Old Bailey sentencing remarks, 21 November 2025
orgs.reach_src: Voice of Europe exposure 2024 (Czech, Belgian and Polish investigations; German politicians investigated) and the Gill case

orgs.n: Shor party carried undeclared Russian money into Moldovan office
orgs.d: Russian money went undeclared into Moldovan elected offices through the party built around businessman Ilan Shor: in August 2025 its governor of the autonomous region of Gagauzia, Evghenia Guțul, was sentenced to 7 years for using undeclared Russian money, and its vice-president Marina Tauber was sentenced to 7½ years in 2025 for illegal party financing. Moldova's Constitutional Court declared the Șor Party unconstitutional on 19 June 2023, and its members have continued under successor parties.
orgs.cite: Constitutional Court of Moldova 2023; Moldovan court sentences 2025

orgs.n: Chinese military-linked association's ex-official advised Czech president
orgs.d: The China Association for International Friendly Contact (CAIFC), which presents itself as a 'friendship' association, is a body under the liaison bureau of the Chinese military's Political Work Department, and one of its former officials became an adviser inside the Czech presidency. Ye Jianming was CAIFC's deputy secretary-general in 2003–2005 and later chairman of the energy company CEFC China Energy, before President Miloš Zeman made him an economic adviser. A 2018 US–China Economic and Security Review Commission report said CAIFC collects intelligence and runs propaganda work. Ye was detained in China in 2018.
orgs.cite: Czech Presidential Office; Reuters reporting on CEFC; Wikipedia 'China Association for International Friendly Contact', citing US–China Economic and Security Review Commission, 2018

orgs.n: Big Four accountants' staff inside governments
orgs.d: The Big Four accounting firms (Deloitte, EY, KPMG and PwC) get their staff inside governments by selling advice to ministries and lending, or 'seconding', employees to them, and the firms' other clients have benefited. In the PwC Australia case of 2023, an Australian Senate inquiry found that a PwC partner who advised the Treasury on new tax laws shared the confidential plans inside PwC to win business from clients avoiding tax. The UK Public Accounts Committee criticised in 2013 the practice of staff seconded to the Treasury. In South Africa, KPMG withdrew a 2017 report it had written for the tax service SARS. The firms also audit most large companies.
orgs.cite: Australian Senate inquiry 2023; UK Public Accounts Committee 2013; Parliament of Australia, joint committee report, Chapter 2 'The PwC breach of confidentiality obligations', 2023

orgs.n: Bain helped Zuma's allies weaken South Africa's tax service
orgs.d: Bain & Company, a US management-consulting firm founded in Boston in 1973, worked from inside South Africa's tax service, the South African Revenue Service (SARS), with President Jacob Zuma and SARS head Tom Moyane to restructure and weaken it, according to the Zondo Commission, the judicial inquiry into the capture of state bodies, in its Part 1 report of January 2022. South Africa suspended Bain from state work, and the UK barred it from government contracts in 2022, lifting the bar in 2023.

orgs.n: Uber Technologies
orgs.d: Uber is a US ride-hailing company that, according to leaked internal files, got serving and former officials to act for it while it operated in breach of local taxi laws. The Uber Files, 124,000 internal documents from 2013–2017 published in July 2022, show Emmanuel Macron, as France's economy minister, working behind the scenes for Uber; after his office was contacted, a Marseille police ban on an Uber service was lifted two days later. Neelie Kroes, the EU's former digital commissioner, helped Uber lobby Dutch ministers, including Prime Minister Mark Rutte, during the cooling-off period that limits such work. Macron said he was proud of supporting the company; Kroes denies wrongdoing.
orgs.cite: The Guardian / ICIJ, Uber Files, July 2022

orgs.n: Greensill founder worked inside Cabinet Office, then hired Cameron
orgs.d: Lex Greensill got inside the UK government as an adviser in the Cabinet Office, the department that runs central government, before founding the supply-chain finance firm Greensill Capital, which lends against invoices. The firm then employed former Prime Minister David Cameron, who lobbied ministers for it in 2020. Greensill collapsed in March 2021, and inquiries in 2021 by the Treasury Committee and by Nigel Boardman for the government examined how its founder's role inside government and Cameron's lobbying gave the firm access.

orgs.n: Odebrecht paid officials in 12 countries
orgs.d: Odebrecht, a Brazilian construction and engineering group renamed Novonor in 2020, paid officials in 12 countries to win public works contracts, running the payments through an in-house bribery unit it called the 'Structured Operations Division'. In December 2016 it admitted to US, Brazilian and Swiss authorities that it had paid $788 million in bribes, and it paid a record fine. The case led to convictions of presidents and ministers in Peru, Ecuador and elsewhere in Latin America.
orgs.reach_src: US DOJ statement of facts (Wikipedia summary)

orgs.n: Privinvest paid Mozambique's finance minister over hidden debts
orgs.d: Privinvest, an Emirati-Lebanese shipbuilding group owned by Iskandar Safa (died 2024), paid Mozambique's Finance Minister Manuel Chang $7 million, US prosecutors said, while supplying boats under $2 billion in state-guaranteed loans that were hidden from the country's parliament and the IMF (the 'hidden debt' deals). Chang was tried in New York in 2024. London's High Court let Mozambique recover over $825 million from Safa's estate and companies.
orgs.cite: US v. Chang (E.D.N.Y.) 2024; UK High Court 2024

orgs.n: Goldman Sachs
orgs.d: Goldman Sachs bankers paid bribes to officials in Malaysia and Abu Dhabi to win work arranging bond issues for 1MDB, Malaysia's state investment fund, from which money was then diverted. Goldman's Malaysian unit pleaded guilty in the US in October 2020, and the bank agreed to pay more than $2.9 billion to US authorities; it settled separately with Malaysia for about $3.9 billion in July 2020. Its staff and former staff have often moved into top finance posts in governments, and former European Commission President José Manuel Barroso chaired its international arm from 2016.
orgs.cite: Goldman–Malaysia settlement July 2020; EU ethics committee Oct 2016; OCCRP, 'Goldman Sachs Pleads Guilty to $1 Billion Bribery Scheme Charges', October 2020

orgs.n: Glencore paid officials in Africa and Latin America
orgs.d: Glencore, a Swiss-based commodity trader and miner founded as Marc Rich + Co, paid officials in several African and Latin American countries to obtain oil, mining rights and favourable treatment. In 2022 it pleaded guilty to bribery in the US and UK, and agreed to pay the Democratic Republic of Congo $180 million to settle claims there.
orgs.reach_src: UK SFO statement of facts; DRC settlement

orgs.n: Gunvor's payments reached officials in three countries
orgs.d: Gunvor, a Geneva-based oil trader, gained its business through payments that reached officials in Côte d'Ivoire, the Republic of Congo and Ecuador. Swiss authorities penalised it in 2019 for failing to prevent bribery in Côte d'Ivoire and the Republic of Congo, and in 2024 it paid about $661 million to US and Swiss authorities over corruption involving Ecuador's state oil business.

orgs.n: Trafigura bribed Petrobras and Angolan officials
orgs.d: Trafigura, a commodity trader founded in 1993, paid officials at state oil companies to win business. It pleaded guilty in the US in 2024 to bribing officials of Petrobras, Brazil's state-controlled oil company, and was convicted in Switzerland in 2025 over bribes to an Angolan official (the Swiss verdict is under appeal).
orgs.cite: US DOJ 2024; Swiss Federal Criminal Court 2025

orgs.n: SNC-Lavalin got Trudeau to press the Attorney General
orgs.d: SNC-Lavalin, a Canadian engineering company renamed AtkinsRéalis in 2023, got Canada's prime minister to act for it inside government while it faced bribery charges over work in Libya. It lobbied Ottawa for a deferred-prosecution law, which lets a company pay penalties instead of going to trial, and Canada's Conflict of Interest and Ethics Commissioner found in August 2019 that Prime Minister Justin Trudeau improperly pressed the Attorney General to use it for the company.
orgs.cite: Conflict of Interest and Ethics Commissioner, Aug 2019

orgs.n: Adani charged with $250m bribery scheme for Indian officials
orgs.d: The Adani Group, an Indian conglomerate in ports, airports, power and mining founded by Gautam Adani, was charged by US prosecutors in November 2024 with promising over $250 million in bribes to Indian officials to win solar power supply contracts. The charges, against Adani and associates, were filed in New York because the scheme was hidden from US investors. Kenya cancelled its deals with Adani the next day.

orgs.n: FirstEnergy paid Ohio Speaker's group $60m for bailout law
orgs.d: FirstEnergy, an Ohio electric utility, funnelled about $60 million to a group around Ohio House Speaker Larry Householder, the leader of the state's lower house, in return for passing HB 6, a law that bailed out its nuclear plants with charges on customers' bills. Federal prosecutors brought the case, and FirstEnergy paid a $230 million penalty in 2021 under an agreement admitting the scheme.

orgs.n: ComEd gave jobs to Illinois Speaker's allies
orgs.d: Commonwealth Edison (ComEd), Chicago's electric utility owned by Exelon, gave jobs and contracts to associates of Illinois House Speaker Michael Madigan to win his support for laws it wanted. It admitted the scheme in a 2020 deferred prosecution agreement, a deal in which a company admits wrongdoing and pays a penalty to avoid trial. Madigan, the longest-serving speaker of a US state legislature, was convicted in February 2025.
orgs.cite: US Attorney N.D. Ill.; verdict Feb 2025

orgs.n: Firm tied to Duterte adviser won ₱8.68bn pandemic contracts
orgs.d: Pharmally Pharmaceutical Corp., a company founded in 2019 with ₱625,000 in capital, won ₱8.68 billion in Philippine pandemic supply contracts, and a Senate inquiry linked it to Michael Yang, a former economic adviser to President Duterte, raising the question of whether a presidential insider steered state purchasing to it. The Senate Blue Ribbon Committee, which investigates misconduct by officials, held the inquiry in 2021–22.

orgs.n: Macau developer Ng Lap Seng bribed UN General Assembly president
orgs.d: Ng Lap Seng, owner of the Macau property group Sun Kian Ip, bribed John Ashe while Ashe was President of the UN General Assembly, the body of all UN member states, to back a UN conference centre Ng wanted to build in Macau. A New York federal jury convicted Ng in 2017.

orgs.n: Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation
orgs.d: The Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation is a private US charity, founded in 2000, that steers the work of the World Health Organization (WHO), the UN's health agency, through the money it gives. In 2020 it was the WHO's second-largest contributor, supplying 45% of the WHO's funds from non-state bodies, about 12% of WHO operating spending. Most of this money is earmarked, meaning the WHO may spend it only on programmes the foundation picks.
