Large withdrawals from its branches in Brasília and Belo Horizonte, made through firms of publicist Marcos Valério, went to deputies, their relatives or advisers so that they would back the Workers' Party government. In 2012 Brazil's Supreme Federal Court convicted the bank's president, Kátia Rabello, of money laundering and other crimes. The Central Bank of Brazil put the bank into liquidation in 2013.
orgs.cite: Supreme Federal Court AP 470; Portuguese Wikipedia 'Kátia Rabello'

orgs.n: Espírito Santo bank payments linked to Portugal's ex-PM Sócrates
orgs.d: Banco Espírito Santo (BES) was the Portuguese bank of the Espírito Santo family, led by Ricardo Salgado, nicknamed 'Dono Disto Tudo' ('owner of all this'). In the Operation Marquês case, prosecutors link Espírito Santo group payments to former Prime Minister José Sócrates, saying the head of government received undue money, and charge Salgado with corruption. A judge threw out most charges in 2021, an appeal court reinstated them in 2024 and the trial began in July 2025; the defendants are presumed innocent. The bank collapsed in August 2014 and its good assets became Novo Banco.

orgs.n: Lebanon's political class owns the banks that financed the state
orgs.d: In Lebanon, politicians and their families own most of the large commercial banks, which in turn lent heavily to the state those politicians ran. A 2016 study by economist Jad Chaaban found that 18 of the 20 largest banks had major shareholders linked to political elites, holding about 43% of the sector's assets, and that this affected the banks' lending and their exposure to public debt. The banks financed the state and the central bank, the Banque du Liban, under governor Riad Salameh, until the system collapsed in 2019 and froze depositors' savings.

orgs.n: CIA secretly owned Crypto AG, the cipher firm governments trusted
orgs.d: The CIA, the US foreign intelligence and covert-action agency, secretly owned, with West Germany's BND intelligence service, the Swiss company Crypto AG, whose cipher machines more than 120 governments used to protect their messages. The two services bought it in 1970; the BND left around 1993 and the CIA remained owner until 2018. The machines were rigged so the services could read customers' communications. A Swiss parliamentary inquiry confirmed the arrangement in 2020. In October 2025 President Trump confirmed he had authorised the CIA to carry out covert action inside Venezuela.
orgs.cite: Swiss parliamentary inquiry 2020; Trump statement Oct 2025

orgs.n: Crypto AG: cipher firm secretly owned by the CIA and BND
orgs.d: Crypto AG was a Swiss maker of cipher machines (devices that encrypt messages) that was secretly owned by the CIA and West Germany's BND intelligence service, so that the two agencies could read the messages of the governments that bought them. More than 120 governments were customers. The BND co-owned it from 1970 until about 1993 and the CIA until 2018, when the firm was liquidated. The machines were deliberately weakened. A Swiss parliamentary inquiry confirmed the secret ownership in 2020.
reach_est: more than 120 customer states, not all named

orgs.n: India's RAW cultivated Australian politicians and police
orgs.d: India's foreign intelligence agency, the Research and Analysis Wing (RAW), cultivated Australian politicians and a state police service and recruited an Australian with a security clearance, according to Australia's security service ASIO. In a 2021 speech ASIO chief Mike Burgess described a foreign 'nest of spies' that did this and also monitored a diaspora community. In April 2024 Australian media and the Washington Post reported that the country was India and that two RAW officers were expelled in 2020. A RAW officer was also charged in the US over a plot to murder Sikh activist Gurpatwant Singh Pannun.
orgs.reach_src: cases in this file and existing records

orgs.n: Pakistan's ISI funded secret lobbying in Washington
orgs.d: Pakistan's main military intelligence agency, the Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI), secretly funded lobbying of the US Congress and, the US says, used a militant group as its own arm inside Afghanistan's Taliban. US prosecutors said the ISI paid at least $3.5 million to Ghulam Nabi Fai's Kashmiri American Council in Washington to lobby officials and make political donations; Fai pleaded guilty in 2011. That year the top US military officer, Admiral Mike Mullen, called the Haqqani network the ISI's 'veritable arm'; after 2021 its leader Sirajuddin Haqqani became the Taliban government's interior minister. Pakistan denies the ties.

orgs.n: Egyptian intelligence agent inside Germany's federal press office
orgs.d: Egypt's main intelligence service, the General Intelligence Service (GIS), had an agent working inside the German government's press office, which handles the chancellor's communications. German federal prosecutors charged the employee in November 2020 with working for the GIS since 2010, reporting on German media coverage and helping an attempt to recruit a further source, in return for favours for his family.

orgs.n: Cuban intelligence placed agents in the US government
orgs.d: Cuba's foreign intelligence service, the Intelligence Directorate (DI, formerly DGI), recruited people who rose inside the US government and helped run Venezuela's military counterintelligence. It recruited Ana Montes, who became the Defense Intelligence Agency's senior Cuba analyst and spied for Havana until her 2001 arrest; she was convicted in 2002. Former US ambassador Víctor Manuel Rocha also served Cuban intelligence. Under 2008 agreements seen by Reuters, Cuba's defence ministry oversaw the restructuring of Venezuela's military counterintelligence, which turned to watching Venezuela's own officers.
orgs.reach_src: cases in this file and existing records

orgs.n: North Korea's RGB placed hidden IT workers inside foreign firms
orgs.d: North Korea's main foreign intelligence and cyber body, the Reconnaissance General Bureau (RGB), places North Korean IT workers under false identities in jobs inside foreign companies to earn money for the state, according to US agencies. One US 'laptop farm' let such workers appear to be working from the US for more than 300 American companies, earning over $17 million; its American operator was jailed for eight years in 2025. US agencies also tie the RGB to the 2016 theft of $81 million from Bangladesh's central bank through fraudulent SWIFT payment orders sent from inside the bank's network.

orgs.n: Russia's FSB swapped urine samples inside the Sochi testing system
orgs.d: Russia's domestic security service, the FSB, got inside the anti-doping testing at the 2014 Sochi Winter Olympics to hide Russian athletes' drug use. The McLaren reports, commissioned by the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) in 2016, found a 'state-directed' system in which FSB-linked staff, working with Russia's sports ministry and the WADA-accredited Moscow laboratory, opened supposedly tamper-proof sample bottles and swapped athletes' urine. The findings led to sanctions on Russian sport.

orgs.n: National Intelligence Service (NIS), South Korea
orgs.d: The National Intelligence Service (NIS), formerly the KCIA, is South Korea's intelligence agency, and US prosecutors charged that it recruited a Washington foreign-policy expert to work for it. Sue Mi Terry, a former CIA analyst and fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, a leading US think tank, was indicted in July 2024 as an unregistered foreign agent acting for the NIS since 2013. Prosecutors said she passed notes from a 2022 private meeting with Secretary of State Antony Blinken and wrote op-eds at NIS request, in return for designer goods and over $37,000 for her programmes. In October 2026 the charges were deferred; she acknowledged contacts but no wrongdoing.

orgs.n: Srivastava Group network
orgs.d: The Srivastava Group is an Indian company group that EU DisinfoLab, a Brussels research group, linked to a network using UN-accredited NGOs to get speakers into the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva, where they promoted Indian interests and criticised Pakistan. NGOs with UN accreditation may speak at Council sessions. The network, reported in 2019 and in December 2020 as 'Indian Chronicles', revived dead NGOs, impersonated dead rights activists and ran hundreds of fake local news sites; it also worked on the European Parliament. EU DisinfoLab did not show that the Indian government directed it.

orgs.n: Iran Experts Initiative
orgs.d: The Iran Experts Initiative was a project of Iran's Foreign Ministry, begun in 2014, to cultivate Iranian-heritage academics at Western think tanks, research groups that advise governments, so that they would promote Tehran's positions. Leaked ministry emails reported by Semafor and Iran International in September 2023 revealed it and said it was proposed by diplomat Saeed Khatibzadeh. Pentagon official Ariane Tabatabai was linked to it, and House Armed Services chairman Mike Rogers objected. In October 2023 the Pentagon said she had been properly vetted and kept her security clearance.

orgs.n: World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA)
orgs.d: The World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) is the foundation, run jointly by the Olympic movement and governments, that sets drug-testing rules for world sport, and Russia's FSB security service and Ministry of Sport worked through a WADA-accredited laboratory to hide doped athletes. Richard McLaren's reports for WADA in 2016 found a 'state-directed failsafe system' involving the ministry, the FSB and the Moscow laboratory. FSB-linked staff opened supposedly tamper-proof sample bottles at the 2014 Sochi Olympics to swap urine. More than 1,000 Russian competitors benefited between 2011 and 2015, and at least 643 positive samples were hidden. Russian military intelligence hackers later attacked WADA.

orgs.n: World Athletics president took money to hide Russian doping
orgs.d: World Athletics (formerly the IAAF), the governing body of track and field based in Monaco, had its president paid by Russian interests to hide Russian athletes' doping. Lamine Diack led it from 1999 to 2015. In September 2020 a Paris court convicted him of corruption for helping cover up Russian doping in return for money; about €3.2 million was extorted from suspected dopers so they could compete at London 2012.

orgs.n: UN Secretariat and offices pressed and reached by member states
orgs.d: The UN Secretariat in New York and UN offices such as the human rights office (OHCHR) in Geneva have been pressed or reached by member states. In 2016 Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon removed the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen from his list of parties that kill and maim children, citing 'undue pressure' from supporters who threatened to stop funding UN programmes; Saudi Arabia denied making threats. An OHCHR staff member, Emma Reilly, alleged the office confirmed to China the names of Chinese activists attending UN meetings; OHCHR rejected her claims. Snowden documents also showed the NSA got into the UN's internal video system in 2012.

orgs.n: Israeli intelligence spied on and pressured ICC prosecutors
orgs.d: The International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague, the permanent court that tries individuals for genocide and war crimes, was spied on and its prosecutors privately pressured by Israeli intelligence for nearly a decade, according to a May 2024 investigation by the Guardian, +972 Magazine and Local Call. It reported that Mossad director Yossi Cohen pressed prosecutor Fatou Bensouda before she opened a Palestine investigation, and that the communications of Bensouda and her successor Karim Khan were intercepted. Israel denied the claims.

orgs.n: Citizenship sales: buyers paid for passports and diplomatic posts
orgs.d: Countries that sell citizenship or passports have let buyers pay their way into political circles and diplomatic posts. Al Jazeera reported in 2019 that an Iranian donor to Dominica's prime minister was given an ambassadorship and diplomatic passport, and that in Grenada businessmen were offered diplomatic posts; both governments deny wrongdoing. In the 2020 'Cyprus Papers', the Speaker of the House was filmed offering to help a convicted money launderer get a passport. In Comoros, ex-president Sambi was convicted in 2022 over the sale of passports to stateless Gulf residents (bidoon), and FinCEN warned in 2014 that sanctioned Iranians had bought St Kitts passports.
orgs.cite: FinCEN FIN-2014-A004; Al Jazeera Investigative Unit; OCCRP

orgs.n: Zuneth Sattar firms paid Malawi officials for police and army contracts
orgs.d: Companies linked to UK businessman Zuneth Sattar won Malawi police and army contracts by paying officials, according to Malawi's Anti-Corruption Bureau. Its June 2022 report said five companies linked to him won 16 contracts worth over 150 million dollars from the police and the Malawi Defence Force in 2017–2021. The Bureau later arrested Vice President Saulos Chilima, accusing him of receiving about $280,000 and other items from Sattar in 2021 in return for helping two Sattar companies get government contracts. President Chakwera withdrew Chilima's delegated powers; Chilima denied wrongdoing and died in a plane crash in June 2024.
orgs.cite: Malawi ACB report, June 2022; TheCable / AFP, 'Malawi vice-president arrested over $280,000 bribery allegation', Nov 2022; VOA, 25 Nov 2022

orgs.n: Cocaine networks bought military chiefs in Guinea-Bissau and Suriname
orgs.d: Groups moving South American cocaine to Europe and the US, including Colombia's FARC rebels, have bought or recruited military and security chiefs in transit countries. In Guinea-Bissau, former navy chief José Américo Bubo Na Tchuto was arrested in a US sting in 2013 and pleaded guilty, and army chief Antonio Indjai was indicted for offering to store FARC cocaine. In Suriname, Dino Bouterse, head of the counter-terrorism unit and son of the president, was convicted in New York and sentenced in 2015 to about 16 years.

orgs.n: Benjamin Bol Mel and his companies
orgs.d: Benjamin Bol Mel is a South Sudanese businessman whose company held government contracts, and he moved into the country's top offices. He heads ABMC Thai-South Sudan Construction, which received government road contracts worth tens of millions of dollars without competitive bidding, and he was President Salva Kiir's principal financial adviser and private secretary. The US sanctioned him for corruption on 21 December 2017. He was named one of South Sudan's vice presidents and deputy secretary general of the ruling SPLM on 10 February 2025, and was removed from both posts by decree on 12 November 2025.

orgs.n: Danish plant builder paid Mauritian officials in power tender
orgs.d: Burmeister & Wain Scandinavian Contractor, a Danish power-plant builder, paid officials of the Mauritian administration through intermediaries during tenders for the Saint-Louis power station of the state Central Electricity Board, the African Development Bank found. In June 2020 the bank, which lends for such projects, debarred the company from its contracts for 21 months.

orgs.n: Al-Qaeda affiliates inside Afghanistan's Taliban government
orgs.d: Al-Qaeda, the jihadist network founded by Osama bin Laden, has members inside Afghanistan's Taliban government, according to UN monitors. The UN Security Council's sanctions Monitoring Team assessed in 2023 that at least three key leaders in the Taliban government are affiliated with al-Qaeda, and its reports through 2025 say the group keeps close ties with the Taliban and a presence in several provinces.

orgs.n: Zhao Wei crime group runs Laos's Golden Triangle zone
orgs.d: The Zhao Wei Transnational Criminal Organization, a Chinese-led casino group (Kings Romans), runs a Lao government economic zone. Under a 99-year lease from Laos from 2007, Zhao Wei's group set up and administers the Golden Triangle Special Economic Zone in Bokeo province. In 2018 the US Treasury designated the group for drug trafficking and money laundering through the zone, meaning US persons may not deal with it; the UN drugs office has linked the zone to cyber-fraud compounds.

orgs.n: Telecom firms paid the Uzbek president's daughter for licences
orgs.d: Three telecom groups, VimpelCom, Telia and MTS, paid companies controlled by Gulnara Karimova, the Uzbek president's daughter, to get into Uzbekistan's mobile market. In US foreign-bribery settlements in 2016, 2017 and 2019 the firms admitted the payments, agreeing to pay 795, 965 and 850 million dollars respectively. Uzbek prosecutors put her kickbacks at 869.3 million dollars; she was convicted in Uzbekistan in 2017 and 2020.

orgs.n: Businesspeople bribed Marshall Islands lawmakers for a special zone
orgs.d: Cary Yan and Gina Zhou, China-born businesspeople, paid Marshall Islands legislators and other officials from 2016 to 2020 to pass a law creating a semi-autonomous 'Rongelap Atoll Special Administrative Region' that they would shape. Both pleaded guilty to bribery in New York and were sentenced in 2023, Yan to 42 months.

orgs.n: Getax charged with bribing Nauru's politicians for phosphate
orgs.d: Getax Australia, a Gold Coast phosphate trader, is charged by Australian federal prosecutors with conspiring to bribe Nauruan politicians between 2007 and 2012 to win phosphate deals; the case has been repeatedly delayed and the charges are unproven. In a related case, Sydney businessman Mozammil Bhojani pleaded guilty to paying over 120,000 dollars to a Nauruan MP and a minister and was jailed in 2018.

orgs.n: Australian detention contractors' payments reached Pacific politicians
orgs.d: Firms paid by Australia's Home Affairs department to run asylum centres on Nauru and Manus Island passed money to Nauruan and Papua New Guinea political figures, a 2023 Sydney Morning Herald and Age investigation reported. It found millions in subcontracts going to firms tied to Nauru's leaders, including over 120,000 dollars in suspect payments to justice minister David Adeang, who denies wrongdoing; the reporters said they were not claiming the payments were bribes. A former Paladin director said a 1.5 million dollar invoice marked 'Visas' on the Manus contract was a bribe, which Paladin's former chief executive denies.

orgs.n: Habilaj family cannabis network
orgs.d: The Habilaj family ran an Albanian-Italian cannabis-trafficking group, and its link reached Albania's interior minister, Saimir Tahiri, who was in charge of the police and is a cousin of the family. Italian police arrested Moisi Habilaj in October 2017 in a probe into the group, which moved over 3.5 tonnes of cannabis, and wiretaps mentioned Tahiri. On 19 September 2019 Albania's Serious Crime Court convicted Tahiri of abuse of office and sentenced him to 3 years and 4 months, but dropped the drug-trafficking and organised-crime charges.

orgs.n: Hungary's MOL bribed Croatia's PM for control of INA
orgs.d: MOL, Hungary's state-influenced oil company, paid Croatia's prime minister to give it management control of Croatia's national oil company INA, according to Croatian courts. They found that Prime Minister Ivo Sanader took a 10 million euro bribe from MOL chief executive Zsolt Hernádi; the Supreme Court confirmed the conviction in 2021. Hungary has not handed Hernádi to Croatia, and MOL denies the bribe.

orgs.n: Avia Baltika owner's donations bought Lithuania's president
orgs.d: Yuri Borisov, a Russian businessman who ran the Lithuanian helicopter firm Avia Baltika, bought access to Lithuania's president with campaign money. He reportedly gave about 400,000 dollars to Rolandas Paksas's 2002 campaign and then received Lithuanian citizenship by Paksas's decree. In 2004 the Constitutional Court found Paksas had broken the constitution and his oath, and parliament removed him from office, the first European head of state impeached.

orgs.n: 17 Black: planned payments to Malta's top officials
orgs.d: 17 Black, a Dubai company owned by Maltese businessman Yorgen Fenech, was named in leaked papers as a planned source of payments to secret Panama companies of the Maltese prime minister's chief of staff Keith Schembri and energy minister Konrad Mizzi. Journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia exposed the companies and was murdered in 2017; Fenech is charged with commissioning the killing. Schembri and Mizzi resigned, and a 2021 public inquiry found the state had created an 'atmosphere of impunity'.

orgs.n: Dmitry Rybolovlev
orgs.d: Dmitry Rybolovlev is a Russian billionaire who owns AS Monaco football club and was suspected of courting Monaco officials, including former public prosecutor Jean-Pierre Dreno, to get favourable treatment. The suspicion rested on messages from the phone of his lawyer, Tetiana Bersheda. In November 2018 he was made a formal suspect in a corruption and influence-peddling probe, known as 'Monacogate'. The case was dismissed in 2023, and in February 2025 Monaco's courts closed it, ruling the phone data unlawfully obtained after a European Court of Human Rights finding.

orgs.n: 'Conto Mazzini': bribes to San Marino politicians for licences
orgs.d: In San Marino, business owners paid politicians for building permits and banking licences, with the bribes run through a bank account in the name of 'Giuseppe Mazzini', a 19th-century Italian patriot. Twenty-one former political figures, including former state secretaries, went on trial in 2015; several were convicted in 2017 and the convictions were upheld in 2022.

orgs.n: Patria accused of bribing Slovenia's PM for an arms deal
orgs.d: Patria, a Finnish state-owned defence company, was accused of paying bribes, partly aimed at Slovenian Prime Minister Janez Janša, to win a 2006 deal for armoured vehicles. A Ljubljana court convicted Janša in 2013, but the Constitutional Court annulled the verdict and the case lapsed. An Austrian court convicted a middleman, and two Patria executives were convicted in Finland over separate Croatian deals.

orgs.n: Stanford's bank bribed Antigua's financial regulator
orgs.d: Allen Stanford's offshore bank, Stanford International Bank in Antigua, bribed the island's chief financial regulator to look away from a 7 billion dollar fraud. A 2009 US indictment charges Leroy King, head of Antigua's Financial Services Regulatory Commission, with taking more than 100,000 dollars from Stanford to ignore the bank's real assets and obstruct a US investigation; Antigua extradited him in 2019. Stanford was convicted in the US.

orgs.n: MS-13's secret prison deal with Salvadoran officials
orgs.d: MS-13 (Mara Salvatrucha), a transnational gang, made a secret deal with Salvadoran government and prison officials, according to a 2023 US indictment. It says officials gave the gang's jailed leaders benefits and released one wanted by the US, and in return the gang cut public killings and backed the governing Nuevas Ideas party in the 2021 election. The US sanctioned the prisons director in 2021 over the talks; President Bukele's government denies any pact.

orgs.n: Guyana gold firm bribed customs and officials
orgs.d: Mohamed's Enterprise, a Guyanese gold trading firm of Nazar and Azruddin Mohamed, bribed customs and other officials, the US Treasury said when it sanctioned the family and firm in 2024. Treasury said they kept more than 10,000 kg of gold off customs declarations and evaded more than 50 million dollars in duty, paid officials for favourable treatment in court matters and bribed to win state contracts. It also sanctioned a home affairs ministry permanent secretary.

orgs.n: Freemasonry: office-holders in other grand lodges
orgs.hq: London — first grand lodge, 1717; each country has its own grand lodges
orgs.d: This dot gathers Masonic grand lodges not mapped separately; Freemasonry is a fraternal order with private rituals whose members have held senior state and police posts. Cases include presidents who were also grand masters in Gabon, Congo and Liberia, members in UK police lodges named in corruption inquiries, and Cuba's former grand master admitting he was a state-security officer. In the UK, judges and police were for a time required to declare membership, and in 2026 the High Court upheld the Metropolitan Police's rule that officers declare it. Each case names the lodge involved.

orgs.n: Templar order OSTI received Cameroon state oil money via Biya
orgs.d: The Sovereign Order of the Initiatic Temple (OSTI), an esoteric Templar order founded by Raymond Bernard, former head of the Rosicrucian order AMORC in France, received Cameroon state money through President Paul Biya. Le Monde reported in 1999 that Biya gave OSTI and its charity CIRCES tens of millions of francs in 1988–92, and that 11.2 million francs moved from the state oil company SNH to Bernard's own account. The presidency called Bernard an 'old friend' and did not comment on the payments.

orgs.n: Shinto political league members fill Japan's cabinets
orgs.d: Shinto Seiji Renmei (Shinto Association of Spiritual Leadership), the political arm of Japan's Association of Shinto Shrines, runs a league of Diet (parliament) members who back its aims, such as constitutional revision and official honours for Yasukuni Shrine; its members fill most cabinet seats. In 2014, 16 of the 19 members of Shinzo Abe's cabinet were listed supporters, and in 2025, 12 ministers of Sanae Takaichi's new cabinet belonged to its league. It works closely with Nippon Kaigi, a nationalist lobby.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.n: Koreagate: KCIA paid US congressmen through Tongsun Park
orgs.d: South Korea's intelligence agency, the KCIA, paid members of the US Congress in the 1970s through businessman Tongsun Park to keep US support for President Park Chung-hee's government. In 1978, under immunity, Park admitted giving money to 30 members. Former Representative Richard Hanna pleaded guilty and went to prison, and the House reprimanded three other members; former Representative Otto Passman was acquitted.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.n: PRC officials acting through people inside foreign institutions
orgs.d: This dot gathers cases in which officials or intelligence officers of the People's Republic of China worked through local people inside other countries' institutions, where the record does not name the United Front Work Department (the Communist Party body for overseas influence). Cases include the mayor of Arcadia, California pleading guilty in 2026 as a PRC agent, a European Parliament member's aide jailed in Germany in 2025 for spying for China, a former New York police sergeant convicted in 2023 of helping China's 'Fox Hunt' campaign, and Chinese officers placed inside Pacific police forces.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.n: Foreign states paying or recruiting officials (several states)
orgs.d: This dot gathers cases where foreign governments, rather than a single named organisation, paid, recruited or placed people inside another country's institutions. Cases include US Senator Bob Menendez, convicted in 2024 as an agent of Egypt; a Twitter manager convicted in 2022 of spying for Saudi Arabia; Hungary's EU mission running a spy ring against the European Commission; and Canada's parliamentary intelligence committee (NSICOP) finding some parliamentarians 'witting' in foreign interference.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.n: White supremacist groups placing members in US police
orgs.d: Organised white supremacist groups, such as the Klan and skinhead groups, have tried to get their members into police forces, the FBI warned. A 2006 FBI assessment described 'ghost skins' who hide their beliefs and said at least one group urged them to seek police jobs, which 'can lead to investigative breaches'. A 2015 FBI policy guide said investigations of such extremists had often found active links to law enforcement officers.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.n: Know Nothings' secret order took the Massachusetts legislature
orgs.d: The Order of the Star Spangled Banner, a secret anti-immigrant fraternal order, built the Know Nothing movement and its American Party and took over a state government. In the 1854 Massachusetts election it won the governorship, all 40 state Senate seats and all but three House seats. The 1855 legislature passed laws to deport poor or mentally ill Irish residents, to 'inspect' Catholic schools and convents and to require Protestant Bible reading in public schools.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.n: Tammany Society's Grand Sachem Tweed ran New York City
orgs.d: The Society of St. Tammany, a fraternal society with ritual offices called sachems, ran New York's Democratic Party machine and through it the city government. William M. 'Boss' Tweed became its Grand Sachem in 1863 and controlled the city while holding seats in Congress, the county board and the state Senate. A city committee in 1877 estimated he stole $25–45 million; he was convicted in 1873 on 204 of 220 counts.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.n: Orange Order members ran Toronto and held Canada's top office
orgs.d: The Loyal Orange Institution (Orange Order), a Protestant fraternal lodge, had its members fill Canadian city halls and federal office. Twenty of Toronto's 23 mayors in the 19th century and every mayor in the first half of the 20th century were Orangemen, and in 1942 16 of 23 city council members were. Four prime ministers, including Mackenzie Bowell, a past Grand Master, were Orangemen.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.n: Ordre de Jacques-Cartier placed members in Canadian public posts
orgs.d: The Ordre de Jacques-Cartier, a secret French-Canadian Catholic society active from 1926 to 1965, worked by recruiting decision-makers and getting its members appointed to federal public-service jobs. Its members included Montreal mayor Jean Drapeau and politician Pierre Laporte, and it had about 11,300 members in 1955–56. It dissolved in 1965 after a former insider, Roger Cyr, exposed it in a 1964 book.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.n: Knights of St Columbanus members in Ireland's 1948 cabinet
orgs.d: The Knights of Saint Columbanus, a Catholic fraternal order founded in Ireland in 1915 and long described as secretive, had members in Irish cabinets and the civil service. Taoiseach (prime minister) John A. Costello and other ministers in his 1948 government were Knights, and Justice Minister Seán MacEoin reportedly assured the order's Supreme Council that conflict between Church and State would be avoided. These accounts rest mainly on biographies by John Cooney (1999) and Anthony Jordan (2007).
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.n: SAC: Gaullist parallel network that recruited police officers
orgs.d: The Service d'Action Civique (SAC), a Gaullist security association created in 1960 and run in practice by Jacques Foccart, de Gaulle's adviser on Africa, was a parallel network that recruited police officers. Its Marseille leader was himself a police inspector, Jacques Massié, whom an SAC commando murdered with his family in 1981. A National Assembly inquiry followed and the government dissolved the SAC in 1982 under the law on private militias.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.n: Westland New Post had members inside Belgian police and NATO
orgs.d: Westland New Post, a Belgian far-right paramilitary group founded by Paul Latinus, had members inside the gendarmerie (national police) and a NATO site. A former gendarme said he was recruited into 'Group G', a neo-Nazi cell inside the gendarmerie linked to the group, and NATO documents passed on by a member from the Evere transmission centre were found at another member's home. Latinus had been an informant for Belgium's State Security service. A parliamentary inquiry found no proof of a conspiracy behind the Brabant killings.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.n: Reichsbürger coup group with a judge and soldiers inside
orgs.d: The 'Patriotic Union' around Heinrich XIII Prinz Reuss, part of the Reichsbürger movement that rejects the modern German state, had a sitting judge, a former MP and special-forces soldiers among its members. Birgit Malsack-Winkemann, a Berlin judge and former AfD member of parliament, was to be its justice minister and led co-accused through the Reichstag twice in 2022. Federal prosecutors charged the group as a terrorist association planning to storm the parliament; trials began in 2024.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.n: Voice of Europe: Russian-funded payments to European politicians
orgs.d: Voice of Europe was a Prague-based pro-Russian news outlet that, Czech intelligence says, paid European politicians from Russian money supplied by Viktor Medvedchuk. The Czech government sanctioned it in March 2024. German prosecutors are investigating AfD politician Petr Bystroň over cash reportedly handed over in Prague, and both the Bundestag and, in May 2025, the European Parliament lifted his immunity; he denies the claims.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.n: Informationsbyrån (IB)
orgs.d: Informationsbyrån (IB) was a secret Swedish military intelligence bureau with no official status that registered and infiltrated far-left groups, and it was reported to answer to leaders of the governing Social Democratic Party as well as to the military. Journalists Jan Guillou and Peter Bratt revealed it on 3 May 1973, including break-ins at the Communist Party's offices. Former security chief P. G. Vinge wrote that IB director Birger Elmér had regular contact with Prime Minister Olof Palme and reported to party secretary Sven Andersson; Palme denied any link. The journalists, not IB staff, were convicted of espionage in 1974. A 2002 public inquiry set out IB's operations.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.n: White Hand officers' society made its leader Yugoslav PM
orgs.d: The White Hand (Bela ruka), a secret Serbian officers' society founded in 1912 by Petar Živković, gained influence over the future King Alexander and put its leader in charge of government. Alexander suspended the constitution in 1929 with White Hand officers' support, and Živković was made prime minister, serving until 1932.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.n: P3 secret association sought influence over Italian judges
orgs.d: P3 was a secret group, named by the press after the P2 lodge, that Italian prosecutors said sought undue influence on the state, including senior judges. In 2018 a Rome court convicted businessman Flavio Carboni and Arcangelo Martino under the 1982 Anselmi law, which bans secret associations, and gave a senior judge, Vincenzo Carbone, a suspended sentence for abuse of office.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.n: P4: Bisignani network traded confidential state information
orgs.d: P4 is the press name for an information-trading network run by go-between Luigi Bisignani, which drew in officials who passed on confidential state information. In the 2011 inquiry, deputy and former prosecutor Alfonso Papa was accused of passing confidential information to Bisignani; he was convicted in 2016, but the charges lapsed on appeal. Bisignani took a plea of 1 year 7 months.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.n: Mafia-linked secret lodges in Italian local government
orgs.d: In Italy, mafia groups such as the 'Ndrangheta have used 'covered' (secret) Masonic lodges to link up with officials, business and local government. A 2017 report by parliament's Anti-Mafia Commission found 193 lodge members recorded in organised-crime cases and that in Castelvetrano 4 of 5 town executives were Freemasons. In 2023 former senator Giancarlo Pittelli, described as a Freemason linking a clan to Masonic circles, was given 11 years for collusion.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.n: IDEA secret officers' society behind Greece's 1967 junta
orgs.d: IDEA (Sacred Bond of Greek Officers), a secret society of army officers formed in 1945, placed its members at the head of the state through the 1967 coup. Several coup leaders, including Georgios Papadopoulos, were members, and IDEA members took key posts under the junta. In 1975 the junta leaders were convicted of high treason.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.n: Golden Dawn: neo-Nazi party with ties inside Greek police
orgs.d: Golden Dawn, a Greek neo-Nazi party that held up to 21 seats in parliament, had ties inside the police and was ruled a criminal organisation. In 2013 the Council of Europe's human rights commissioner said he had strong evidence of police links to the party, and after the 2012 election polling stations used by Attica police officers gave it just over 20% of the vote. In 2020 an Athens court convicted its leaders of running a criminal organisation, upheld on appeal in 2026.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

channels.n: Ambrosiano money: Milan → Nassau → Lima → Managua
channels.d: Banco Ambrosiano ran its offshore business through Ambrosiano Overseas in Nassau and Banco Ambrosiano Andino in Lima, and funded both the Somoza regime and the Sandinista opposition in Nicaragua. The Vatican Bank was its main shareholder. When it collapsed in 1982, $1.287 billion could not be accounted for.

channels.n: IOR settlement: Vatican City → Ambrosiano creditors in Milan
channels.d: Archbishop Marcinkus's IOR allegedly issued letters of patronage backing Ambrosiano's foreign units. The IOR denied legal liability but acknowledged 'moral involvement' and paid US$224 million to the creditors.
channels.cite: Wikipedia 'Institute for the Works of Religion'

channels.n: Calvi's flight: Milan → London (Blackfriars Bridge, 1982)
channels.d: Roberto Calvi, Ambrosiano chairman and P2 member, fled Italy on a false passport as the bank failed. He was found hanging from Blackfriars Bridge on 18 June 1982; Italian authorities reopened it as murder and prosecuted Licio Gelli and Giuseppe Calò.

channels.n: P2 lodge: Arezzo/Rome → Buenos Aires
channels.d: Gelli held an honorary diplomatic post at Argentina's Rome embassy and had ties to Perón and the junta. P2 members in Argentina included junta member Emilio Massera and Social Welfare Minister José López Rega, founder of the Triple A death squad; Raúl Lastiri was briefly interim president in 1973.

channels.n: P2 lodges in South America: Rome → Montevideo / São Paulo / Caracas
channels.d: P2 had lodges in Uruguay, Brazil and Venezuela as well as Argentina and Chile. Gelli took refuge in Uruguay in 1981 after his list was found.

channels.n: Gelli's escape: Arezzo → Geneva (1982–88)
channels.d: Gelli was arrested in Geneva in 1982 while trying to withdraw money, escaped prison in 1983, surrendered in 1987 and was extradited to Italy in 1988.

channels.n: Stay-behind coordination: NATO ACC/CPC → Rome (Gladio)
channels.d: NATO's Clandestine Planning Committee and the Allied Clandestine Committee coordinated national stay-behind plans. Andreotti said the last ACC meeting took place on 23–24 October 1990 under Belgian General Van Calster, the day before he disclosed Gladio and its 622 listed members to parliament.

channels.n: Stay-behind coordination: NATO ACC → Ankara (Counter-Guerrilla)
channels.d: Turkey's stay-behind branch was the Counter-Guerrilla, whose existence Prime Minister Bülent Ecevit revealed in 1973. Former prosecutor Emin Değer documented its ties to the Grey Wolves.

channels.n: Stay-behind coordination: NATO ACC → Athens (LOK / Sheepskin)
channels.d: Greece's network was the LOK mountain raider units, with a branch called Operation Sheepskin; the Greek defence minister said it operated until 1988.

channels.n: Stay-behind coordination: NATO ACC → Brussels / The Hague / Copenhagen
channels.d: Belgium's parliamentary committee found the ACC coordinated networks in ten countries. Dutch PM Ruud Lubbers informed parliament of a secret organisation in the defence ministry in 1990; arms caches were found near Rozendaal (1983) and Velp. Denmark's network was Absalon.

channels.n: WACL / Taiwan covert aid: Taipei → Tegucigalpa (Contras)
channels.d: After the 1987 Iran-Contra revelations, reports showed Taiwanese covert military aid to the Contras, who were based in Honduras; League chairman Ku Cheng-kang reportedly helped arrange it and Taiwan's Foreign Ministry confirmed the activity.

channels.n: CAUSA: New York → Contras in Honduras / Nicaragua
channels.d: CAUSA International, founded by the Unification movement in New York in 1980 and active in 21 Latin American countries, aided the Nicaraguan Contras.

channels.n: Unification Church: Seoul → Tokyo (dissolution case)
channels.d: Japan holds a large share of the church's membership. The Tokyo District Court ordered the Japanese religious corporation dissolved on 25 March 2025; the order was upheld in 2026.

channels.n: Snow White: Saint Hill → Los Angeles → Washington (IRS, Justice Dept)
channels.d: The Guardian's Office, headquartered at Saint Hill Manor in England with a US base in Los Angeles, ran infiltration of US federal agencies. The FBI caught two operatives in a federal courthouse in 1976 and raided church offices on 8 July 1977; eleven executives were convicted in 1979.
channels.cite: United States v. Hubbard; Wikipedia 'Operation Snow White'

channels.n: Snow White: Saint Hill → Toronto (infiltration of public offices)
channels.d: Operation Snow White extended to Canada. In 1992 the church was convicted in Ontario of breach of public trust for infiltrating public offices.
channels.cite: R. v. Church of Scientology of Toronto (1992)

channels.n: Gülen movement base: İzmir → Saylorsburg, Pennsylvania (1999)
channels.d: The movement began in İzmir, where Gülen set up student boarding houses from 1966; it moved its base to Pennsylvania in 1999, where Gülen lived until his death in October 2024.

channels.n: School seizures: Ankara → Bishkek (Sapat schools to Maarif)
channels.d: After 2016 Turkey pressed governments to close or hand over Gülen-linked schools. Kyrgyzstan transferred management of the Gülen-linked Sapat schools to Turkey; Turkey's Maarif Foundation said in 2021 it had taken over 216 schools in 44 countries.
channels.cite: Stockholm Center for Freedom; Turkish Minute (2021)

channels.n: Brotherhood branches → Hamas: Cairo / Amman → Gaza
channels.d: Hamas began in 1987 as a Brotherhood offshoot. On 13 January 2026 the US Treasury designated the Egyptian and Jordanian branches as Specially Designated Global Terrorists for support to Hamas.
channels.cite: US Treasury designation 13 Jan 2026 (Times of Israel)

channels.n: Hizb ut-Tahrir coup attempts: Jerusalem → Amman / Damascus (1968–69)
channels.d: The party, founded in Jerusalem in 1953, was allegedly involved in two failed coup attempts in Jordan and Syria in 1968–69, and in Egypt in 1974.

channels.n: Le Cercle: Paris → Bonn (founding axis)
channels.d: Antoine Pinay and Jean Violet founded the circle in 1952–53 with Konrad Adenauer and Franz Josef Strauss; Franco-German reconciliation was an early aim.

channels.n: Le Cercle: Paris / London → Pretoria (apartheid delegation)
channels.d: South Africa sent the only official government delegation to the circle; in the 1970s–80s it was tied to the apartheid state and backed Renamo and UNITA.

channels.n: Bilderberg → Val-Duchesse dinner: Oosterbeek → Brussels (2009)
channels.d: In November 2009, outside its annual conference, Bilderberg held a dinner at the Château of Val-Duchesse in Brussels to promote Herman Van Rompuy's candidacy for President of the European Council.

channels.n: Trilateral Commission → Carter administration: New York → Washington
channels.d: The commission was founded in 1973 at David Rockefeller's insistence. By 1980, 21 former members held posts in the Carter administration, including Carter, Mondale, Brzezinski and Defense Secretary Harold Brown.

channels.n: CFR War and Peace Studies: New York → State Department
channels.d: During the Second World War the council's confidential War and Peace Studies group, funded by the Rockefeller Foundation, wrote 682 classified memoranda for the State Department.

channels.n: Young Global Leaders → heads of government: Cologny → Ottawa / Paris / Wellington / Helsinki
channels.d: Alumni of the WEF's Young Global Leaders programme who later led governments include Justin Trudeau (Canada), Emmanuel Macron (France), Jacinda Ardern (New Zealand) and Sanna Marin (Finland).

channels.n: Mont Pelerin members in office: Mont Pèlerin → Bonn / Rome / Prague / Santiago / Colombo
channels.d: Society members who held top office include Ludwig Erhard (West German economics minister and chancellor), Luigi Einaudi (President of Italy), Václav Klaus (Czech president), Carlos Cáceres (Chilean finance minister) and Ranil Wickremesinghe (Sri Lankan prime minister).

channels.n: Stand Your Ground: Tallahassee → ALEC model bill (Arlington) → ~30 states
channels.d: Florida passed its Stand Your Ground law in 2005; ALEC then adopted a model bill with the same wording, and similar laws spread to about 30 states with ALEC's support.

channels.n: BCCI: Luxembourg → London → Washington (First American Bankshares)
channels.d: BCCI, registered in Luxembourg and run from London and Karachi, secretly controlled Washington's First American Bankshares through nominee investors; Clark Clifford was its chairman. The Kerry–Brown Senate report found Clifford and Robert Altman closely involved with BCCI from 1978 to 1991.
channels.cite: Kerry–Brown report to the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, 1992

channels.n: BCCI: London → Panama City (Noriega accounts)
channels.d: BCCI was accused of laundering money for Panama's Manuel Noriega; bankers Amjad Awan and Syed Hussain reportedly managed his accounts.

channels.n: United Front: Beijing → London (Christine Lee alert, 2022)
channels.d: In January 2022 MI5 issued an interference alert to MPs naming solicitor Christine Lee as suspected of acting for the United Front Work Department.

channels.n: United Front: Beijing → Ottawa / Vancouver (Canada)
channels.d: A February 2022 Canadian court ruling found the UFWD's Overseas Chinese Affairs Office engaged in covert intelligence gathering; a Privy Council Office warning described Chinese interference as likely to be persistent and pervasive.

channels.n: United Front: Beijing → New York (Liang Litang indictment, 2023)
channels.d: The US sanctioned UFWD head You Quan in January 2021, and in May 2023 indicted Liang Litang as an illegal agent; senators asked the Justice Department to investigate 'Overseas Chinese Service Centers' in seven cities.
channels.cite: US Treasury sanctions 2021; US DOJ indictment 2023

channels.n: Chinese-linked donors: Beijing → Sydney / Canberra (Dastyari, 2016–17)
channels.d: A Chinese company with government links paid $44,000 of Senator Sam Dastyari's legal bills in 2014; he later took positions at odds with Australia's South China Sea policy and warned donor Huang Xiangmo his phones were likely tapped. He announced his resignation on 12 December 2017.

channels.n: Susurluk: Ankara → Susurluk crash (1996)
channels.d: Grey Wolves second-in-command Abdullah Çatlı died in the November 1996 Susurluk car crash; the scandal exposed ties between the group, the Counter-Guerrilla and state officials.

channels.n: Black Hand: Belgrade → Sarajevo (1914)
channels.d: Apis allegedly decided to have Archduke Franz Ferdinand killed; three young Bosnian Serbs were recruited, trained and smuggled from Serbia into Bosnia. The assassination on 28 June 1914 helped set off the July Crisis.

channels.n: Aum Shinrikyo: Tokyo → Moscow → Podgorica
channels.d: Aum built a Russian following; a 2000 plot to free Asahara involved a Russian member. Russia opened a criminal case and banned the group in 2016, the same year Montenegro expelled 58 foreigners linked to it.

channels.n: The Fellowship: Washington → Kampala (prayer breakfast)
channels.d: Journalist Jeff Sharlet tied Fellowship associates to Uganda's proposed anti-gay bill with a death penalty, which a member denied. In 2023 the Fellowship paid for a US congressman's keynote at Uganda's National Prayer Breakfast.

channels.n: The Fellowship: Moscow → Washington (Butina, 2017)
channels.d: Maria Butina, who later admitted acting as an undeclared Kremlin agent, helped arrange Russian attendance at the 2017 National Prayer Breakfast; the FBI interviewed organiser Doug Burleigh about her.

channels.n: El Yunque: Puebla → Madrid (HazteOír)
channels.d: Álvaro Delgado linked El Yunque to Spain's HazteOír and CitizenGo; in 2014 a Madrid judge said evidence possibly showed links between HazteOír members and El Yunque but could not confirm the organisation exists.

channels.n: Sangh overseas: Nagpur → Nairobi (1947) → London
channels.d: The RSS's overseas wing began in Nairobi on 14 January 1947 as the Bharatiya Swayamsevak Sangh, later the Hindu Swayamsevak Sangh, with branches in Kenya, the UK, Australia and Nepal.

channels.n: Gulen-linked teachers removed or targeted for removal to Turkey, 2017–2021
channels.d: Malaysia deported three Turks to Turkey on 11 May 2017; an attempt to fly Veysel Akcay out of Ulaanbaatar was stopped on 27 July 2018 when Mongolian authorities grounded the plane; Orhan Inandi was taken from Bishkek to Turkey in mid-2021, which Erdogan announced on 5 July 2021.
channels.cite: Al Jazeera 12 May 2017; Euronews 28 July 2018; 24.kg 17 August 2021

channels.n: Gulen schools handed to Turkey's Maarif Foundation — Pakistan
channels.d: Pakistan's Supreme Court ordered on 28 December 2018 that Pak-Turk schools be transferred to the Turkiye Maarif Foundation.

channels.n: Moon group money into Uruguay's Banco de Crédito, 1981–2002
channels.d: Moon's group bought 49% of Banco de Crédito in 1981; Uruguay's parliamentary banking commission found the bank lent about US$100 million to Moon-linked companies before it closed in 2002.

channels.n: Taizhou Taiwan Affairs Office tours for Chiayi village chiefs, 2023
channels.d: The Taizhou Taiwan Affairs Office paid lodging and local travel for Chiayi village and ward chiefs on 2023 trips organised by Lin Hsueh-feng, convicted 28 May 2025.

channels.n: CIA money to the Congress for Cultural Freedom
channels.d: The CIA's International Organizations Division paid for the Paris secretariat, which subsidised magazines and national committees in about 35 countries until 1966-67.

channels.n: CIA via Free Trade Union Committee to European unions
channels.d: CIA money passed through the AFL's Free Trade Union Committee to Irving Brown in Paris and on to Force Ouvrière, Italian unions and port groups.

channels.n: USAID and AIFLD to Brazilian union trainees
channels.d: USAID contracts funded AIFLD's training institutes in Brazil, whose graduates its director said took part in the 1964 conspiracy.

channels.n: CIA to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty
places: National Committee for a Free Europe, New York
channels.d: Covert CIA funds flowed through the New York committee to the Munich stations, which broadcast into the Soviet bloc until open funding began in 1971-74.

channels.n: Ford Foundation: Jakarta to Berkeley and back to the cabinet
channels.d: Ford grants sent University of Indonesia economists to Berkeley; they returned to run BAPPENAS and the finance ministry from 1967-68.

channels.n: US aid: Santiago to Chicago and back to the junta
channels.d: US aid, then Ford money, paid for 126 Chilean economists to train at Chicago in 1955-73; from 1975 they held Pinochet's economic ministries.

channels.n: Red Notice requests from member governments to Lyon
channels.d: Governments file notices with the General Secretariat in Lyon; notices later found political were refused or deleted, sometimes after arrests abroad.

channels.n: Rio 2016 vote payment to an IOC member
channels.d: Brazilian prosecutors say $2 million was routed through businessman Arthur Soares to Lamine Diack before the IOC chose Rio in Copenhagen in October 2009.

channels.n: Tobacco companies to WHO through partners
channels.d: The Zeltner Committee traced tobacco-company work through consultants, food subsidiaries and other UN bodies aimed at WHO tobacco control.

channels.n: Milner's Kindergarten: London → Cape Town / Johannesburg, 1901–1910
channels.d: Milner brought Oxford graduates from London into the Cape High Commission and the Transvaal and Orange River Colony administrations (1901–05); most returned to London in 1909–10 after the Union, while Duncan and Feetham stayed in South Africa.

channels.n: Round Table groups: London → dominion capitals, 1909–1915
channels.d: Lionel Curtis toured the dominions in 1910–11 setting up local Round Table groups (Canada, South Africa, Australia, New Zealand; Newfoundland 1912). Quigley adds India and a loose US group by 1915. City placement for each dominion group is approximate.
channels.cite: Wikipedia 'Round Table movement'; Quigley, Tragedy and Hope, p. 950

channels.n: Hotel Majestic, Paris 1919 → Chatham House (London) and CFR (New York)
channels.d: On 30 May 1919 British and American delegation experts at the Hotel Majestic proposed an Anglo-American institute; the British side founded Chatham House (1920) and the American side merged with a New York group to form the Council on Foreign Relations (1921). Quigley says Chatham House treated the CFR as its American branch.
channels.cite: Chatham House (2019); CFR centennial history (2021); Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, pp. 182–191

channels.n: Chatham House → dominion institutes of international affairs, 1927 onward
channels.d: Quigley writes that Chatham House set up branch institutes in each dominion, each formed around the local Round Table members, the earliest in Canada and Australia in 1927, with the question taken up at the 1933 Toronto Commonwealth relations conference. Dates for each institute are not verified here.
channels.cite: Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, ch. 10, p. 191

channels.n: Morgan–Lazard axis: New York ↔ London
channels.d: Quigley describes the 'chief backbone' of the network as financial cooperation between the Morgan bank in New York and London financiers led by Lazard Brothers and Morgan, Grenfell; he says Milner refused a Morgan partnership in London in 1901 and that Brand and then Adam Marris were managing directors of Lazard. This is Quigley's account.

channels.n: Institute of Pacific Relations conference circuit, 1925–1936
channels.d: IPR conferences met at Honolulu (1925, 1927), Kyoto (1929), Shanghai (1931), Banff (1933) and Yosemite (1936). Quigley says the British and dominion delegations were drawn from the same Milner Group circles as the Commonwealth relations conferences.
channels.cite: Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, ch. 10; Wikipedia 'Institute of Pacific Relations'

channels.n: UAE–Amdjarass–Darfur supply route to the RSF (UN panel)
channels.d: A UN Panel of Experts report leaked in January 2024 found 'credible' evidence that the UAE flew weapons to Sudan's Rapid Support Forces several times a week through the airstrip at Amdjarass in northern Chad, from where supplies crossed into Darfur. The UAE says its 122 flights carried humanitarian aid.
channels.cite: UN Panel of Experts on Sudan (Jan 2024), reported by Al Jazeera

channels.n: Russian military air bridge Syria–eastern Libya for Wagner
channels.d: UN monitors and US Africa Command reported Russian military flights from Syria to eastern Libya supplying Wagner and Haftar's forces in 2019–20, including 338 flights counted in one UN report and Syrian fighters recruited by Wagner flown in on at least 33 Cham Wings flights. Russia later used eastern Libyan bases as logistics hubs for Africa Corps.
channels.cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya; AFRICOM, as summarised on Wikipedia

channels.n: Gupta money route: South African state contracts to Dubai
channels.d: The leaked #GuptaLeaks emails showed funds from the Free State government's Vrede dairy project laundered through Dubai paid for the family's 2013 Sun City wedding. A South African Council of Churches and academics' report estimated about R40 billion moved to Dubai from state-company deals in 2011–2017. The family moved to Dubai in 2016.
channels.cite: News24 #GuptaLeaks (2017); SACC report (2017), as summarised on Wikipedia

channels.n: Chinese police outposts in the Americas
channels.d: Outposts that Safeguard Defenders attributed to the Fuzhou city and Qingtian county police. The Manhattan site led to US convictions (2024, 2026); the RCMP closed its Quebec probe in 2025 without charges; no Latin American government has reported findings.
channels.cite: Safeguard Defenders reports, 2022; Wikipedia 'Chinese police overseas service stations'

channels.n: Indian intelligence plots against Sikh activists in North America
channels.d: Canada linked agents of India's government to the killing of Hardeep Singh Nijjar and expelled six diplomats; US prosecutors charged RAW officer Vikash Yadav with directing a plot to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun in New York and said he sent video of Nijjar's body to the go-between.
channels.cite: Government of Canada, October 2024; US v. Yadav and Gupta (S.D.N.Y.)

channels.n: Egypt and Qatar to Senator Menendez
channels.d: Prosecutors showed bribes flowing to Senator Menendez in return for help to the Egyptian government and for favourable words about Qatar to secure Qatari royal investment for a New Jersey developer; convicted 16 July 2024.

channels.n: Russian Interior Ministry police training in Central America
channels.d: Russia's Interior Ministry runs a police training centre in Managua for Nicaraguan and regional officers; the US Treasury sanctioned it on 15 May 2024.

channels.n: China's Ministry of Public Security police cooperation in the Pacific
channels.d: China's Ministry of Public Security has embedded officers in Fiji's police (2013–2024), sent advisory teams to the Solomon Islands (from 2022), Kiribati and Vanuatu (from 2023), and supplied equipment and training in China.
channels.cite: East Asia Forum, 7 March 2024; RFA/BenarNews, 20 March 2024

channels.n: Prince Group assets seized across Asia and London
channels.d: After the US and UK acted against Chen Zhi on 14 October 2025, the UK froze 19 London properties, Singapore seized S$150 million, Taiwan seized NT$4.5 billion and Hong Kong HK$2.75 billion.
channels.cite: US DOJ / UK sanctions, October 2025, as summarised on Wikipedia

channels.n: Baku to PACE Strasbourg and Milan — caviar diplomacy payments
channels.d: Money from Azerbaijan-linked companies reached PACE members, including €2.39 million to Italian Luca Volontè (convicted in Milan, 2021) and payments to German members whose immunity the Bundestag lifted in 2021.
channels.cite: PACE Independent Investigation Body 2018; Court of Milan 2021

channels.n: Azerbaijani Laundromat — Baku through Danske Bank Tallinn
channels.d: About $2.9 billion moved in 2012–2014 from Azerbaijani sources through four UK-registered shell companies with accounts at Danske Bank's Estonian branch.

channels.n: Doha and Rabat to Brussels — Qatargate cash
channels.d: Belgian investigators say cash from Qatar and Morocco reached the European Parliament through former MEP Pier Antonio Panzeri and his NGO Fight Impunity.

channels.n: Moscow Metropol to Milan — Lega oil-deal talks
channels.d: October 2018 Metropol hotel meeting on an oil deal meant to finance the Lega; case dismissed in 2023.

channels.n: Medvedchuk network — Prague hub to European parliaments
channels.d: Voice of Europe was run from Prague and used Belgium as a hub for meetings and payments; German prosecutors in Munich investigate an MEP; in London, Nathan Gill was convicted of taking bribes passed on for Medvedchuk.
channels.cite: Czech Security Information Service 2024; Old Bailey 2025

channels.n: Ankara to Pristina and Chișinău — renditions of Gülen-linked teachers
channels.d: Six Turks were flown from Kosovo to Turkey in March 2018 and seven teachers from Moldova in September 2018; Kosovo's spy chief was later convicted and the European Court of Human Rights ruled against Moldova.
channels.cite: Basic Court of Pristina 2023; ECtHR Ozdil and Others v. Moldova 2019

channels.n: Odebrecht bribery network across Latin America and Africa
channels.d: In its December 2016 plea agreement Odebrecht admitted paying $788 million in bribes in 12 countries between 2001 and 2016 through its Structured Operations Division.

channels.n: Glencore bribes paid in five African states (UK SFO case)
channels.d: The UK Serious Fraud Office found more than $28 million in bribes paid by Glencore's UK oil arm in Nigeria, Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea, Côte d'Ivoire and South Sudan in 2012–2016.
channels.cite: UK SFO, Southwark Crown Court, June 2022

channels.n: Unification Church honours and fees to heads of government
channels.d: From its Seoul headquarters the Unification Church, through the Universal Peace Federation and the Sunhak Peace Prize, gave a governance award to Cambodia's sitting prime minister (2019), a US$1 million-class peace prize to Senegal's sitting president (2020) and speaking fees of $2–2.5 million to Donald Trump (2021–22).

channels.n: Universal Church from Brazil to Angola
channels.d: The UCKG's Brazilian leadership placed bishops in Brazil's Congress, cabinet and Rio City Hall, and ran the church in Angola until the Angolan government removed its Brazilian leaders in 2020.
channels.cite: Wikipedia 'Universal Church of the Kingdom of God'

channels.n: US Christian lobbies and Uganda's anti-gay laws
channels.d: Journalist Jeff Sharlet reported that David Bahati, chair of Uganda's Fellowship-linked National Prayer Breakfast, floated his 2009 bill at the 2008 breakfast; an activist named Family Watch International's president as a lobbyist for the 2023 Act.

channels.n: Crypto AG: Swiss machines, readers in Langley and Pullach
channels.d: Cipher machines made in Zug were sold to governments in more than 120 countries while the CIA (Langley) and BND (Pullach) owned the firm and read the traffic.

channels.n: Marsalek network: Moscow to Munich, Vienna and London
channels.d: Former Wirecard COO Jan Marsalek, now in Russia, directed a Bulgarian spy cell in London and took material from Austrian intelligence officer Egisto Ott.

channels.n: North Korean IT workers: China border to US laptop farms
channels.d: Kejia Wang met a North Korean contact in Shenyang and Dandong and ran US laptop farms; Christina Chapman ran another in Arizona. Workers abroad logged in through the farms to US company networks.

channels.n: Russian money through Moldovan courts to Latvian banks (Global Laundromat)
channels.d: Russian firms 'guaranteed' fake debts, Moldovan judges ordered them paid into Moldindconbank, and the money moved on through Latvian banks to shell companies, many registered in the UK, in 2010–14.
channels.cite: OCCRP and Novaya Gazeta, Global Laundromat

channels.n: Calabrian and Sicilian betting money through Malta licences
channels.d: Italian investigations found mafia groups collecting bets in Italy through companies licensed by the Malta Gaming Authority, hiding ownership behind fiduciaries.

channels.n: Casamance rosewood through Banjul to China
channels.d: Rosewood logged in Senegal's Casamance was trucked into The Gambia and shipped from Banjul; The Gambia exported about $163 million to China in 2014–17.
channels.cite: TRIAL International (2019); EIA 'Cashing in on Chaos' (2020)

channels.n: Kokang scam bosses handed from Laukkai to Chinese courts
channels.d: Myanmar handed Kokang family leaders to China in 2023–24; the Bai group was tried in Shenzhen and the Ming family in Wenzhou, and members of both were executed in early 2026.

channels.n: Rotterdam cocaine fugitive to Freetown
channels.d: Dutch police believed Jos Leijdekkers lived in Turkey before Reuters placed him in Sierra Leone in 2025.

channels.n: Rothschild five-house network
channels.d: Mayer Amschel Rothschild's five sons set up cooperating houses in Frankfurt, London, Paris, Vienna and Naples, which moved government money across Europe, including British war subsidies before 1815.
channels.cite: Quigley, Tragedy and Hope p. 51; Wikipedia 'Rothschild family'

channels.n: Morgan axis: 23 Wall Street–Morgan, Grenfell–Morgan, Harjes
channels.d: J.P. Morgan & Co. worked with its London affiliate (J.S. Morgan & Co., later Morgan, Grenfell) and Paris affiliate (Morgan, Harjes); in 1914–17 this axis handled British and French war purchasing and loans in the US. Quigley calls the New York–London tie to Lazard Brothers 'the chief backbone' of the Round Table organisation.
channels.cite: Wikipedia 'J. P. Morgan', 'American entry into World War I'; Quigley, Tragedy and Hope p. 951

channels.n: Jekyll Island to the Federal Reserve Board
channels.d: New York bankers from Morgan, National City and Kuhn, Loeb travelled with Senator Aldrich to Jekyll Island in November 1910 to draft the Aldrich Plan; the Federal Reserve Act followed in 1913 and Paul Warburg joined the Board in Washington in 1914.
channels.cite: Federal Reserve History, 'The Meeting at Jekyll Island'

channels.n: Goldman Sachs to treasuries and central banks
channels.d: Former Goldman Sachs partners and staff moved into the US Treasury and White House (Rubin, Paulson, Cohn), the Bank of Italy, ECB and Italian premiership (Draghi, Monti), the Bank of Canada, Bank of England and Canadian premiership (Carney) and the German finance ministry (Kukies).
channels.cite: Wikipedia biographies of Rubin, Paulson, Cohn, Draghi, Monti, Carney, Kukies

channels.n: Lazard London to wartime Washington
channels.d: Quigley traces Lazard Brothers men (Robert Brand, Thomas Brand, Adam Marris) into Britain's wartime missions and embassy in Washington, 1940–46.

channels.n: Schiff's Japanese war loans
channels.d: Jacob Schiff met Bank of Japan deputy governor Takahashi Korekiyo in Paris in April 1904 and floated about $200 million of Japanese war bonds in New York.

channels.n: Credit Suisse–Privinvest–Maputo tuna-bond loans
channels.d: Loans arranged by Credit Suisse bankers in London went to Mozambican state companies for Privinvest contracts; kickbacks flowed back to the bankers through UAE companies.

channels.n: Rigged Crypto AG machines to customer governments
channels.d: Crypto AG sold cipher machines to more than 120 governments while secretly owned by the CIA and BND; Iran is one named customer.
